# ItalyBlueCard – full text

## Already Have a Blue Card in Germany or Another EU Country? Moving to Italy
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/blue-card-mobility-move-from-another-eu-country.html
Summary: How Blue Card holders from other member states can work in Italy: short business stays, long-term mobility after twelve months, and what the Italian employer must file.
One of the strengths of the EU Blue Card is mobility. If you already hold one in Germany, the Netherlands or another member state, moving to Italy is easier than starting from scratch. Article 27-quater sets out how.
Short stays for work   A Blue Card holder from another member state can enter and stay in Italy for business activities for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. This covers meetings, projects and temporary assignments related to your job. Check the exact scope of “business activity” for your case before you plan a longer project.
Moving to Italy for good   After twelve months of legal residence as a Blue Card holder in the first member state, you can move to Italy to work without needing a visa. If you are moving from a second member state, the minimum prior residence drops to six months.
Your Italian employer must file the work authorisation application within one month of your entry. The Italian Blue Card conditions apply: qualification, contract of at least six months, and a salary at least equal to the CCNL level and the ISTAT average.
Why people move   A lower salary threshold. Italy’s threshold, reported at about €36,300 a year, is well below Germany’s €50,700 standard threshold for 2026. A move to a role or city with lower pay scales can still keep you on a Blue Card. Family or partner in Italy. Climate, lifestyle, cost of living outside the biggest cities. A company project in Italy. What to consider before leaving the first country   Settlement rights. Germany grants a settlement permit after 27 months of Blue Card employment with A1 German, or 21 months with B1, according to the Berlin immigration service. If you are close, it may be worth finishing that period first. Pension. Contributions paid in EU countries are coordinated, so periods are not lost. Family. Family members who are with you can follow under the Italian rules on reunification; Blue Card holders can apply whatever the permit length. The Italian employer   You still need an employer in Italy. If the company you work for is in Germany and has no Italian entity, an Employer of Record can employ you in Italy. If it is a new Italian company, it can file directly.
Step by step   Confirm you have held the first Blue Card for at least twelve months (six if from a second state). Agree the Italian contract and salary. Enter Italy with your current Blue Card. The employer files the work authorisation within one month. Stay contract, residence permit, tax code, health service, as for any newcomer. What happens to the old Blue Card   Once you have the Italian Blue Card, the old one is no longer the basis of your stay. Tell the authorities in the first country according to their rules, and deregister your address there.
Comparing the three countries   See Italy, Germany or the Netherlands and our comparison page .
Tell us where you hold your Blue Card and when you would like to move.
Two questions before you go   Do I need a new visa to move? Not after the minimum residence in the first state, under the mobility rules. You enter with your current Blue Card.
Is the 90-day rule a permit to relocate? No. It is for business stays. Relocation needs the long-term mobility procedure.
Does my German employer have to be involved? Only if you keep working for it. If so, an EOR can employ you in Italy on its behalf.
What salary will I need? The Italian conditions apply: at least the CCNL level and the ISTAT average gross annual salary, reported at about €36,300.
Can my family move with me? Yes, under the Italian reunification rules. Blue Card holders can apply whatever the length of the permit.
What if I have held my first Blue Card for less than a year? Then you would need the ordinary procedure, starting with a nulla osta and a visa, unless you wait until the twelve months are complete.
Does my German language level matter in Italy? No. Italy has no language requirement for the Blue Card. It only matters if you want to keep the option of the German settlement permit.

## Building a Relocation Package for Italy: Housing, Fringe Benefits and Meal Vouchers
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/relocation-package-benefits-italy-tax-free.html
Summary: What a company abroad can offer a professional moving to Italy, and how the 2026 Italian rules treat housing, fringe benefits, meal vouchers and other items.
A good relocation package does two things: it makes the move financially manageable in the first months, and it uses the Italian rules so that more of what the company spends reaches the employee. Here is what works in Italy in 2026.
One-off support for the move   Common items:
flights for the employee and family; temporary accommodation for the first weeks; shipping of personal goods; visa and document costs: our case fee is €2,500, plus consular fees, translations and apostilles; a settling-in allowance for furniture and deposits. How each item is treated for tax depends on how it is paid: reimbursed against receipts, paid directly by the employer, or as a cash allowance. Reimbursements of documented relocation costs and allowances follow different rules. We structure them in payroll and tell you the effect on net pay before you agree.
Housing   Rent paid or reimbursed by the employer is common in relocation packages. It can be one of the most valuable items for the employee, especially in the first year in a city like Milan. Its tax treatment depends on the structure, so put it in writing and let us set it up.
Fringe benefits   In 2026, fringe benefits such as gift cards, utility bills and fuel are tax-free up to €1,000 a year, or €2,000 for employees with dependent children. For a family that has just arrived, help with utility bills under this rule is simple and appreciated.
Meal vouchers   Meal vouchers (buoni pasto) are exempt from tax and contributions up to €10 a day if electronic, €4 if paper. For a full-time employee they add up to a meaningful tax-free sum over a year.
Supplementary health and pension   Contributions to supplementary health funds are exempt up to €3,615.20 a year. Employer contributions to a supplementary pension fund are tax-efficient. Productivity bonus   If there is a company agreement, productivity bonuses up to €5,000 a year are taxed at a flat 1% in 2026 instead of normal rates.
Language and integration   An Italian course, help with school enrolment, an introduction to a local community: small costs that decide whether a family settles in.
What not to promise   Spouse work rights before the family permit is confirmed. Tax outcomes on items that depend on structure. A fixed start date before the consulate step. A sample structure, without numbers   Before the move: visa and documents, flights, shipping. First month: temporary housing, settling-in allowance. First year: housing support, fringe benefits up to the limit, meal vouchers, language course. Ongoing: supplementary health and pension through the CCNL or company plan. How it reaches the invoice   All of these items run through Italian payroll and appear on the monthly invoice to the company abroad, at cost, with the payslip summary. One-off items are invoiced in the month they occur.
Does it affect the Blue Card threshold?   No. The threshold is checked on gross salary. Benefits do not help reach it, and they do not count against it.
See the cost calculator for the salary side, and ask us to structure the package.
Practical questions   Can the company pay my school fees? It can. The tax treatment depends on structure; some education benefits can fall within company welfare plans. We check before setting it up.
Can benefits be paid in my home currency? Payroll is in euros. The company is invoiced in EUR or USD.
Is a company car common for relocated staff? Less than housing support. It is taxed on a flat share of a standard cost that depends on emissions.
What about a home trip every year? A paid flight home can be part of the package. Its tax treatment depends on how it is structured; agree it in writing and let us set it up in payroll.
Should the package be in the contract? Key items, yes, or in a signed relocation letter. It avoids misunderstandings and lets payroll treat each item correctly from the first month.
Can the company recover costs if I leave early? Some packages include repayment clauses for early departure. They must be agreed in writing and be reasonable; we can include them in the relocation letter.

## Your Italian Pension as a Non-EU Professional: What You Build and When
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/italian-pension-contributions-non-eu-workers.html
Summary: How INPS contributions work for people who move to Italy mid-career, the 2026 retirement rules, the contribution ceiling, and what happens if you leave.
When you become an Italian employee, a share of every payslip goes to INPS, the national social security institute. Most of it builds your state pension. If you moved mid-career and are not sure you will stay forever, it is fair to ask what that pension will be worth to you.
What you pay and what your employer pays   You: 9.19% of gross pay for most private-sector employees, plus 1% on the part above €56,224 a year. Your employer: around 30%, depending on sector, size and contract. These contributions fund pensions, unemployment benefit, sickness and maternity pay, and family allowances. The pension share is the largest.
The contribution ceiling   For people first insured from 1996 onwards, pension contributions stop above an annual earnings ceiling: €122,295 in 2026. That includes anyone who starts working in Italy now. On very high salaries, the part above the ceiling carries no pension contributions on either side.
How the pension is calculated   For people who started after 1995, the Italian pension is calculated on the contributions actually paid over the career, revalued over time, and converted into a pension at retirement. Every year counts in proportion to what was paid.
When you can retire   Under current rules:
old-age pension from 67 with at least 20 years of contributions; early retirement regardless of age after 42 years and 10 months of contributions for men, one year less for women. From 2027 both requirements rise by one month, and from 2028 by three months, according to the secondary source we used.
If you stay a few years and leave   This is the real question for many relocated professionals. Three cases.
You move to another EU country. Contributions paid in EU countries can be coordinated: each country pays its share of the pension, and periods can count towards minimum requirements. You return to a country with a social security agreement with Italy. Agreements may allow periods to be combined. Whether your country has one, and what it covers, needs checking. You return to a country without an agreement. Your Italian contributions remain recorded with INPS and may give a pension at retirement age if the requirements are met. Rules for non-EU workers who leave Italy have specific provisions that we have not verified for this article. Before you move, ask your home pension authority what applies.
The TFR is separate   Your TFR severance, 6.91% of yearly pay set aside by the employer, is not a pension. It is paid when employment ends, or you can direct it to a supplementary pension fund. If you expect to leave Italy, keeping the TFR liquid is often simpler; if you stay, a pension fund can be tax-efficient. Ask us to explain the options before you choose.
Supplementary pension funds   Many CCNLs include a sector pension fund with employer contributions if you join. Personal contributions to supplementary pension funds have tax advantages.
What it means for your offer   When comparing an Italian offer with one at home, remember that part of what looks like a large gap between gross and net is your pension and social insurance. You are not losing it; you are saving it, under Italian rules.
Your records   INPS keeps your contribution record online. Once you have the credentials, check it every year against your CU certificate.
Read more in from RAL to net pay .
Loose ends   Can I get my contributions refunded if I leave? Do not assume a refund. Rules depend on agreements and specific provisions; check with INPS or an adviser.
Do contributions count if I come back to Italy later? Yes, your INPS record stays, and later periods add to it.
Does the employer’s share go to me? It goes to INPS and counts toward your pension, sick pay and other benefits.
Are contributions paid on the 13th month? Yes. The 13th and 14th month carry contributions like normal salary.
Does the TFR count toward the pension? No. The TFR is severance, separate from the state pension, unless you send it to a supplementary pension fund.
Can I check my future pension? INPS offers online simulations once you have access to your record. Run one after your first year to see how your Italian contributions add up.

## Working Remotely from Italy Without a Work Permit: Why It Backfires
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/remote-work-from-italy-without-permit-risks.html
Summary: A non-EU employee who just moves to Italy and keeps working creates immigration, tax and social security problems. What the risks are and the clean alternative.
“I’ll just move and keep working remotely.” We hear this often, from employees and sometimes from their managers. For a non-EU national it is the most expensive shortcut in this whole topic. Here is why, and what to do instead.
The immigration problem   Entering Italy as a visitor does not give a right to work. Working from Italy for your foreign employer is still working in Italy. Without a permit that allows work, you are exposed: fines, refusal of future permits, problems at the border. And when you eventually apply for a proper permit, a history of irregular stay can count against you.
The tax problem   If you live in Italy for most of the year, you are likely to become tax resident. Income earned while working here is taxable here. Without Italian payroll, nobody withholds that tax, and you are responsible for it, with penalties if you do not declare it.
The social security problem   Social security is generally due where the work is physically done. A non-EU employer with no Italian presence, and an employee in Italy with no Italian contributions, is a gap that INPS can fill retroactively.
The company’s problem   For the employer, an employee working long term in Italy can create a taxable presence, a permanent establishment, especially if the person signs contracts or manages local business. And if the arrangement is a contractor agreement, it can be reclassified as employment.
Why people try it anyway   They think the visa process is impossible without an Italian company. They think a short stay is fine, and it becomes long. They hear stories from EU citizens, who can move freely, and assume the same applies. The clean alternative   An Employer of Record solves all four problems at once:
Immigration: the EOR files the work permit, usually the Blue Card , as your Italian employer. Tax: Italian payroll withholds income tax every month. Social security: contributions go to INPS and build your pension. The company: you are employed by the EOR in Italy, not by your company. The company pays a monthly invoice and directs your work. With ItalyBlueCard that costs €250 per month plus your employment cost, and €2,500 for the visa case.
What about EU citizens?   EU citizens do not need a work permit. They still need the tax and social security side handled. The same EOR structure applies, without the visa step.
What about short business trips?   Short trips for meetings or conferences are different from relocating. Rules on business visits depend on your nationality and the activity. Ask before travelling if you are unsure.
What about digital nomad visas?   Italy has introduced a permit for highly qualified remote workers. Its conditions differ from the Blue Card, and it does not make you an Italian employee. We have not verified its current requirements for this article; if it fits your case better, a specialised adviser can help.
If you are already in Italy   If you have already been working from Italy without a permit, do not ignore it. Talk to an immigration lawyer and a tax adviser about regularising your position. Then set up a proper structure going forward.
In short   The shortcut saves a few weeks and creates problems that last years. The proper route is predictable, and an EOR makes it possible without an Italian company. Tell us about your case .
Frequently, people ask   What if I am a dual national with an EU passport? Then you do not need a permit. You still need Italian payroll for long-term work here.
Can I work from Italy during the visa wait? No. Wait in your country of residence until the visa is issued and you have entered with it.
Is it different for a few weeks of holiday with a laptop? Occasional work during a short holiday is a grey area. Avoid anything that looks like moving your work to Italy.
Does the company risk anything if the employee hid the move? Yes. Authorities look at the facts, not at what the company knew. That is why companies increasingly ask staff to declare where they actually work.
How fast can the EOR route be set up? The structure itself is ready in days. The permit then follows the route timeline; the nulla osta for the Blue Card has a 30-day legal deadline.

## Leave in Italy and Long Trips Home: Planning Holidays as a Relocated Employee
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/annual-leave-italy-trips-home-relocated-employees.html
Summary: Four weeks of statutory leave, extra hours under the CCNL, public holidays and the August slowdown: how relocated professionals can plan visits home.
For someone who has moved far from home, leave is not a detail. A wedding in Chennai, the holidays in São Paulo, a parent’s birthday in Ankara: the trips home are often what makes life abroad sustainable. Italy is generous with leave, and a little planning goes a long way.
What you are entitled to   At least four weeks of paid annual leave a year by law. At least two of them must be taken in the year they accrue; the rest within the period set by law and the CCNL. Extra paid hours off (ROL, permessi) under many CCNLs, on top of the four weeks. Public holidays: 12 national holidays plus the local patron saint’s day. Sick leave, maternity and paternity leave separately from annual leave. Leave accrues month by month. In your first months you will have accrued only a part of it. Ask the company employing you whether early use of leave can be agreed if you have an important trip.
Planning long trips   Many relocated employees prefer one long trip a year rather than several short ones. Four weeks plus ROL hours makes a three-week trip realistic, especially if it includes public holidays.
Tips:
Agree dates early with your manager, especially if the team is spread across time zones. Combine with public holidays, both Italian and, when working for a company abroad, your company’s calendar. Check your permit. Make sure it does not expire while you are away, and that you carry the permit or the renewal receipt. Long absences from Italy can matter for permits; ask us if you plan to be away for months. Remote work from abroad during a trip home is a different thing from leave. A few days can usually be agreed; longer periods can change where tax and contributions are due. Ask before. The August question   Many Italian companies slow down or close for part of August. If you work for a company abroad, its calendar applies, not the Italian one. Still, offices and services in Italy are quieter in August, which is worth knowing if you have appointments to schedule.
Unused leave   Leave is meant to be taken. Italian rules limit paying it out instead of taking it, except at the end of employment. When you leave, any unused leave is paid in your final payslip.
Leave and your employer abroad   If the company employing you is used to unlimited or minimal leave policies, explain the Italian rules early. We put them in the contract, track balances in payroll, and include them in the monthly report.
Parental leave   If you have a child in Italy: mandatory maternity leave of five months, paternity leave of ten working days, mostly paid through INPS, plus optional parental leave, partly paid. Tell us as soon as you can so payroll and planning are in place.
Sick leave while abroad   If you fall ill during a trip home, the rules on medical certificates differ from those in Italy. Contact us before you assume it counts as sick leave.
A checklist before every long trip   Dates agreed with your manager Leave balance checked on your payslip Permit valid for the whole trip, or renewal receipt with you Any remote work days agreed in writing Return flight before the permit or receipt expires Read more about contracts, leave and termination .
Questions we hear often   Can I carry leave into the next year? Within limits. Two weeks must be taken in the year of accrual; the rest within the period set by law and the CCNL.
Do I get my home country’s public holidays? Not as a right. You can use leave for them, or the company can agree extra days.
Can I buy extra leave? Not as a standard Italian practice. Unpaid leave can be agreed.
Are Saturdays counted as leave days? It depends on whether your schedule counts five or six working days; the CCNL and your contract set how leave is counted.
What if my manager abroad refuses leave? The four weeks are a legal right, not a perk. We explain the rules to the company employing you, and the leave balance appears in every monthly report.
Can I take all four weeks at once? The law requires at least two weeks in the year of accrual and does not forbid a longer block. It needs your manager’s agreement on dates.

## Degree, Certificates and Translations: Preparing Your Documents for an Italian Work Visa
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/documents-legalisation-translation-italy-work-visa.html
Summary: Which documents a work visa and family file need, how legalisation, apostille and certified translation work, and when a CIMEA statement helps.
In our experience the longest part of a Blue Card case is rarely the authorities. It is the documents: a degree certificate from a university that takes weeks to answer, a marriage certificate in the wrong format, a translation that is not certified. Start this track first, and the rest of the case moves faster.
What you will need   For the work permit and visa:
passport, with enough validity and blank pages for your consulate’s rules; degree certificate and transcripts, or proof of a higher professional qualification; experience letters, if you qualify through experience, describing tasks, level and dates; professional recognition, for regulated professions; proof of accommodation in Italy, such as a lease, a hotel booking or a hosting declaration; the nulla osta issued to your employer. For the family file:
marriage certificate; birth certificates of children; proof of dependency for parents. Legalisation and apostille   Documents issued outside the EU usually have to be authenticated before Italian authorities accept them. Depending on the issuing country, that is done through an apostille or through legalisation by the Italian consulate. The Embassy of Italy in Beijing, for example, asks for a certified copy, an apostille and a certified Italian translation for non-EU documents.
The process depends on the country that issued the document, not on your nationality. A degree from a UK university held by an Indian citizen follows the UK process.
Certified translation   Italian authorities want documents in Italian. Translations must usually be certified: either made or confirmed by the consulate, or sworn in Italy. A translation by a friend, or by an unlisted agency, is not enough.
Translate after the apostille, not before, so the apostille is translated too.
CIMEA statement for degrees   The declaration of value (dichiarazione di valore) issued by the Italian consulate used to be the standard way to describe a foreign degree. According to the Embassy in Beijing checklist, a CIMEA comparability certificate can replace it for higher education qualifications. CIMEA is the Italian centre for academic recognition and mobility, and it can issue statements online. Ask us which option is faster for your country.
Experience letters that work   If your Blue Card relies on experience rather than a degree, the letters carry the case. Each should state:
the employer, on letterhead, with contact details; your role and level; the main tasks, in a few lines; start and end dates, full-time or part-time; signature and date. Dates alone are not enough. Ask former employers early.
Names and spellings   Check that your name is spelled identically on the passport, the degree, the marriage certificate and the tax code. Transliterated names cause the most problems. If there is a difference, get an official document explaining it before you apply.
A timeline   When What As soon as the offer is likely Request degree, transcripts, experience letters, civil certificates When received Apostille or legalisation After apostille Certified translation Before filing Send scans to your employer for the nulla osta At the consulate Originals and copies as listed by your consulate Our part   As your Employer of Record we tell you exactly which documents your route needs, check scans before filing, and keep them consistent across the permit, the contract and payroll. See visa routes or the guide for your country .
The questions that come up   How long does an apostille take? It depends on the issuing country and office. Ask for it as soon as you have the original.
Are digital diplomas accepted? Rules vary. Many consulates still want certified paper originals. Check your consulate’s checklist.
Do I need my high school diploma? Usually not for a Blue Card based on a degree. It may be needed for some recognition procedures.
Can I translate documents myself? No. Translations must be certified, either by the consulate or by a sworn translator in Italy.
Should I bring originals to Italy? Yes. Bring originals with apostille and translation. Offices in Italy may ask to see them again, and family files reuse many of the same documents.
What about documents in English? Even English documents usually need an Italian translation for Italian authorities. Some offices accept English for certain items; do not count on it.

## Do You Need to Speak Italian to Work in Italy on a Blue Card?
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/do-you-need-italian-to-work-in-italy.html
Summary: No language test for the Blue Card, but Italian matters for offices, landlords and daily life. What to expect and how to get started.
“Do I need to speak Italian?” is one of the first questions on every call. The honest answer has two parts: for the permit, no; for life in Italy, it helps a lot.
The permit   The conditions for the Blue Card in article 27-quater are about qualification, contract length and salary. There is no Italian language requirement to obtain it. The same is true for the employment contract: if you work for a company abroad in English, your job can be in English.
Other permits, especially long-term residence permits later on, may involve language requirements. We will cover them when relevant to your case.
The contract   Your Italian employment contract is a legal document under Italian law. We prepare it in Italian and English, so you understand exactly what you sign. In case of doubt, the Italian text prevails, which is normal for a contract governed by Italian law.
Payslips and payroll   Italian payslips use Italian terms: competenze, trattenute, netto, TFR. We explain them once, in English, and answer questions in English afterwards. See your first payslip .
The offices   Immigration desks, the Questura, the municipal registry and local health authorities work in Italian. Some staff speak English, many do not. Forms are in Italian. For the employer-side appointments, such as the stay contract, we are there with you.
Landlords and daily life   Many landlords and agencies in big cities speak English, but leases are in Italian. Doctors in large cities often speak English; pharmacies, shops and neighbours less so. School communications for children will be in Italian.
Most people who move with basic Italian find the first months much easier than those who move with none.
How fast can you learn enough?   That depends on your languages and how much time you invest. Speakers of Spanish or Portuguese find Italian approachable; Brazilians often understand a lot from the start. Speakers of other languages need more time, but basic survival Italian is reachable in a few months of steady practice.
Practical tips   Start before you move. An evening course or an app for a few months before departure pays off on arrival. Learn the admin vocabulary. Words like permesso di soggiorno, codice fiscale, residenza, contratto di locazione, medico di base. You will hear them every day. Take a course on arrival. Many cities have courses for foreigners, some free. Ask your employer. Language training can be offered as a benefit, and an employer-paid course can be structured efficiently. Use your colleagues. If you have Italian colleagues, ask them to speak Italian with you for small talk. For the company employing you   If you want the person to integrate quickly, offer an Italian course as part of the relocation package and give time for it during the first months. It is a small cost compared with the value of an employee who settles in and stays.
What we do   We work in Italian and English, prepare bilingual contracts, explain every document and accompany you to employer appointments. Through our relocation service we can also handle the paperwork in Italian on your behalf. See relocation .
In short   No Italian required for the permit or for an English-speaking job. Some Italian makes the first months easier and the rest of your stay richer. Start early, keep it practical.
Common follow-ups   Will my employer pay for Italian lessons? It can, if agreed. We can run it through payroll.
Is English enough for a doctor’s visit? Often in big cities, less so elsewhere. Bring a translation app and medical vocabulary.
Do children learn fast? Usually much faster than adults. Schools can help with language support.
Is Italian required for the CIMEA statement or documents? Documents must be translated into Italian, but you do not need to speak it. Certified translators handle that.
Will I need Italian for a renewal? The Blue Card renewal is based on your job and salary. Language requirements may matter for other permits later; we will tell you when they become relevant.
Are there English-language public services? Some city portals and services offer English pages, but most procedures are in Italian. Keep a bilingual friend or our team close for the first appointments.

## Italy, Germany or the Netherlands? A Blue Card Comparison for Candidates
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/italy-vs-germany-netherlands-blue-card-candidates.html
Summary: Salary thresholds, permanent residence, and employment rules in three EU Blue Card countries, from the point of view of a non-EU professional choosing where to go.
The EU Blue Card is one scheme with many versions. Every member state that applies it sets its own salary threshold and keeps its own employment law. For a candidate weighing offers, or a company deciding where to place someone, the differences are large. Here is a side-by-side for Italy, Germany and the Netherlands.
Salary thresholds for 2026   Country Standard threshold Reduced threshold Italy ISTAT average gross annual salary and CCNL level; reported at about €36,300 a year (secondary source) - Germany €50,700 a year €45,934.20 for shortage occupations and IT specialists without a degree Netherlands €5,942 gross a month, excluding holiday pay €4,754 a month Sources: IND for the Netherlands; The Local, citing the Federal Foreign Office, for Germany; art. 27-quater and a secondary source for Italy.
The practical consequence: a role paid above the Italian threshold but below the German reduced threshold qualifies in Italy and not in Germany. Early-career graduates, people in sectors with lower pay scales, and professionals from smaller companies often find Italy’s threshold within reach when the others are not.
Permanent residence   Germany is explicit about a fast track: a settlement permit after 27 months of Blue Card employment with basic German (A1), or 21 months with B1, according to the Berlin immigration service. For Italy and the Netherlands we have not yet verified the equivalent rules and do not quote them here.
Speed   Italy sets a 30-day legal deadline for the Blue Card work authorisation. For the other two countries, check the official timelines for your case.
Family   In Italy, a Blue Card holder can apply for family reunification whatever the length of the permit, with income and housing conditions. Family members get a permit of the same length.
Employment rules   Italy Germany Netherlands Paid leave At least 4 weeks; CCNLs often add more - At least four times weekly hours Extra pay 13th month mandatory, 14th under some CCNLs - 8% holiday allowance Sick pay Shared INPS and employer under the CCNL - 70% for up to two years Notice Set by the CCNL Statutory 4 weeks, longer for the employer with tenure - Severance TFR, 6.91% of pay a year, paid at the end - - Blank cells are topics we have not verified for this article. Our comparison page tracks them.
Language   Italian offices work in Italian, German offices in German, Dutch offices often in English as well. In all three, learning the language changes daily life. In Germany it also shortens the path to settlement.
Cost of living   Hard to compare in a table: it depends on the city far more than on the country. Milan and Amsterdam are expensive; Turin, Bologna and Naples are generally cheaper than the German and Dutch hubs. Compare specific cities.
The employer question   In all three countries, you need an employer in the country. If the company that wants you has no entity in Italy, an Employer of Record solves it. That is what we do.
How to decide   If your salary clears all three thresholds, compare cities, languages and career markets. If it clears only Italy’s, the decision is made for you, and it is not a bad one. Check your case .
Answers in a line or two   Can I hold Blue Cards in two countries? You hold one at a time. Mobility rules let you move between member states.
Does Italy count time spent in Germany? EU rules allow some periods in other member states to count for long-term residence. We have not verified the Italian details for this article.
Which country is fastest? It depends on the consulate and the city. Italy’s 30-day legal deadline for the nulla osta is a useful anchor.
Which is best for a family? All three allow family reunification. Compare schools, housing and language support in the specific cities you are considering.
Can I start in Italy and move later? Yes. After twelve months as a Blue Card holder in Italy you can use EU mobility rules to move. See moving with a Blue Card .
Where do salaries go further? That depends far more on the city than the country. Use the net pay calculator for Italy and compare rents in the cities on your list.

## Choosing a City in Italy When You Relocate: Cost, Jobs and Local Tax
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/choosing-italian-city-cost-of-living-newcomers.html
Summary: Milan, Rome, Turin, Bologna, Naples or a smaller town: how newcomers on a work permit can weigh housing, commute, local surcharges and family life.
If you work for a company abroad through an Employer of Record, you often have a choice that local hires do not: where in Italy to live. The permit, the contract and the payroll work the same everywhere. The life around them does not.
The cities most newcomers consider   Milan. The largest international job market and business community. Finance, fashion, design, consulting, tech, pharma. Two airports with long-haul connections. Housing is the main cost. Rome. The capital: public institutions, energy, telecoms, international organisations. A big city with a slower rhythm in some neighbourhoods. Turin. Automotive, aerospace and engineering, with a strong technical university. More space for the money than Milan. Bologna. Machinery, motor brands, food industry and one of Europe’s oldest universities. Compact and well connected by high-speed rail. Naples. Aerospace, shipping and a growing developer scene. Lower living costs. Smaller cities and towns. Many professionals working remotely for foreign companies choose them for housing, space and pace. Local tax: small but real   On top of national income tax, you pay a regional and a municipal surcharge, depending on where you live. They change your net pay, not your employer’s cost. Examples from secondary sources read in October 2026:
Milan’s municipal surcharge is 0.8%, with an exemption for incomes up to €23,000. Rome’s is 0.9%, and the Lazio regional rate reaches 3.33% above €28,000. Naples has the highest municipal rate of the large cities, 1.0%. Bologna applies 0.8%. Turin’s is progressive, from 0.8% to 1.2%. On a €50,000 gross salary, the gap between the cheapest and the most expensive combination of region and city is in the order of €1,000-1,500 a year of net pay. Try your numbers in the net pay calculator .
Housing   Housing is the biggest variable. It also matters for the permit: you need a registered lease for residence registration, and if your family joins, the home must be suitable for the number of occupants. Commuter towns around the big cities offer larger homes for the same rent, with train connections.
Family life   Schools. International schools are concentrated in the larger cities. Public schools teach in Italian everywhere. Health care. The national health service covers residents everywhere; waiting times differ by region. Community. Larger cities have established communities from many countries, which helps in the first months. Work and travel   If your company is abroad, flights matter. Check direct connections to your home country and your company’s hubs. Time zones too: Italy is on CET (UTC+1), CEST in summer.
If you might later look for an Italian job, choose a city with a market for your profile.
Practical questions   Can I move from one Italian city to another later? Yes. You update your residence, and possibly your permit address. Your contract states the place of work; for remote employees we update it.
Does the city affect the Blue Card? No. The threshold is national.
Does the city affect my employer’s cost? No. Surcharges come out of your gross pay.
How to decide   Make a short list of two or three places, spend a few days in each if you can, and compare rent, commute, schools and flights. Ask us for help with the first weeks wherever you choose.
Still wondering?   Which city is best for English speakers? Milan has the largest international community, but English is spoken in professional circles in every major city.
Is public transport good enough to live without a car? In the big cities, yes, for most people. In smaller towns a car is often needed.
Are rents negotiable? Sometimes, especially for longer leases. A strong Italian contract helps your position.
Should I live in the city centre? Centres are attractive but expensive and sometimes noisy. Many families choose well-connected neighbourhoods or nearby towns with a train line.
Can I change my mind after a year? Yes. Your permit is national; moving city means a new lease, a new residence registration and a new family doctor, not a new permit.
Does my Blue Card salary have to be higher in Milan? No. The threshold is the same everywhere, although Milan employers often pay more because of housing costs.

## Non-EU Founders Moving to Italy to Run a Team: Questions and Answers
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/non-eu-founders-relocating-to-italy-faq.html
Summary: You founded a company outside Europe and want to live in Italy while building a team there. How to get a permit, an Italian contract and payroll without opening an entity first.
Founders from India, Brazil, Turkey, China or the US increasingly choose Italy as a European base: for customers, for talent, for quality of life, sometimes for family. Many of them hit the same wall in the first month: as a non-EU national, they need a permit, and a permit needs an Italian employer. Here are the questions we get from founders, with direct answers.
Can I employ myself through my own foreign company?   Not directly. Your foreign company cannot file an Italian work permit unless it has an Italian entity. An Employer of Record can employ you in Italy on behalf of your company, exactly as it would any other employee, provided the employment is genuine: a role, a salary, a contract.
Do I qualify for a Blue Card as a founder?   The Blue Card looks at the qualification, the contract and the salary, not at your title. If you have a degree or qualifying experience, a contract of at least six months, and a salary at or above the threshold (reported at about €36,300), the route is open. Your company must actually pay that salary every month.
Would an Italian startup visa be better?   Italy has specific routes for innovative startups and self-employment. They are different from the employee route, with their own conditions. If your plan is to incorporate in Italy from day one, they may fit. If your company stays abroad and you want to start quickly, the EOR plus Blue Card route is usually simpler. We focus on the second; for the first, a specialised adviser is the right call.
Can my first Italian hires join through the same EOR?   Yes. EU citizens can start within days of a signed offer. Non-EU hires go through the same permit process as you. Each one costs €250 per month plus the employment cost, and €2,500 per visa case if needed.
What about tax?   As an Italian employee you pay Italian income tax and contributions through payroll. Your company abroad may still be taxable in its home country. Living in Italy and directing a foreign company from here can raise questions about where the company is managed, and whether it has a permanent establishment in Italy. Take advice before you move, especially if you are the sole director.
What happens to my shares?   Owning shares in your company is not affected by the employment. Dividends and capital gains are taxed according to your tax residence. Equity granted as part of your employment may have specific treatment. Check with an adviser who knows both systems.
Can my family come?   Yes, under the income and housing conditions, and as a Blue Card holder whatever the length of your permit. See family reunification .
When should I open an Italian entity?   When you have a stable team, need to sign contracts in Italy, or the fixed costs of an entity drop below the sum of EOR fees. We transfer employees without loss of seniority. For Blue Card holders, the first twelve months require labour office approval for a change of employer, so plan the move after the first year if you can. See moving to your own entity .
Which city?   That depends on your market and your hiring plan. Milan for finance, fashion and the biggest international scene; Turin and Bologna for engineering and industry; Rome for public sector and energy; smaller cities for cost and quality of life. See choosing a city .
How long until I can live here?   The Blue Card nulla osta has a 30-day legal deadline. Your own document preparation and the consulate are the variable parts. Plan in months, not weeks.
Where do I start?   Send us your nationality, qualification and the salary your company can pay. We reply with the route and the cost within one business day.
Quick checks   Can I hold an Italian Blue Card and be the director of my foreign company? You can own and direct your company; what matters is that your employment in Italy is genuine. Take tax advice on the director role.

## Moving a Sponsored Employee from an EOR to Your Own Italian Entity
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/move-from-eor-to-own-italian-entity-permit.html
Summary: When the time comes to open your Italian company, how to transfer Blue Card holders without losing seniority or putting the permit at risk.
An Employer of Record is often the first chapter, not the whole story. A company sends one person to Italy, then three, then opens an office. At some point it makes sense to have its own Italian entity. If some of those employees hold Blue Cards, the transfer needs a little more planning than usual.
Why companies move   The Italian team has grown and the entity’s fixed costs are now lower than the sum of EOR fees. The company needs a legal presence to sign contracts, sell or bid for projects. The group wants its own local management and payroll. What the employee keeps   A transfer from the EOR to your entity can be structured so that the employee keeps seniority, accrued leave and the employment history. The CCNL may stay the same or change if the new entity’s activity falls under a different one. The TFR accrued with the EOR is either paid out or transferred, depending on how the transfer is done and where the TFR has been going.
What the permit needs   The Blue Card is linked to the employer. Under article 27-quater, in the first twelve months of legal employment, a change of employer requires the prior approval of the local labour office, deemed given if the office does not reply within 15 days. After twelve months, the holder has equal access to the labour market and the change follows the ordinary communication rules.
In practice:
Transfers after the first year are simpler. If you can wait, wait. Transfers in the first year need the approval request, with the new contract terms, before the switch. In both cases the new employer must meet the Blue Card conditions: salary, qualification match, contract length. At renewal, the permit is renewed with the new employer.
A transfer plan   Set the date. Ideally after the first anniversary for Blue Card holders, and at the start of a month for payroll. Ready the entity. Incorporated, bank account open, registered with the tax agency, INPS and INAIL, payroll set up. Agree terms. Same salary or better, same level or higher, seniority recognised in writing. Permit step. Request labour office approval if within the first year. Close with the EOR. Final EOR payslip with the accrued items or a transfer of them, as agreed. First payslip with the entity. Check it together with the employee. Common mistakes   Starting the new contract before the approval in the first year. Lowering the salary to harmonise with local staff, taking it below the threshold. Forgetting the family: family members’ permits depend on the main permit holder’s status. Leaving the transfer to the last week of the permit’s validity. How we help   As the outgoing employer we prepare the transfer documents, calculate the final or transferred items, and coordinate the permit step with your new entity’s payroll provider. If you want, we can also run the entity’s payroll at €55 per payslip, so nothing changes for the employees except the name of the employer.
Should you keep the EOR for some people?   Sometimes. Companies with people in several Italian cities, or with a mix of long-term staff and short projects, keep some employees with the EOR and move others. There is no rule that everyone must move at once.
In short   Plan the timing around the first year of each Blue Card, keep salary and level at least the same, and do the permit step before the switch. Talk to us when you start planning the entity.
Frequently raised points   Does the employee need a new visa? No, the transfer happens in Italy. The permit is updated, and renewed with the new employer.
Can the new entity use a different CCNL? Yes, if its activity falls under a different one. Check the salary still meets the threshold and the level matches.
What about employees who are EU citizens? Same transfer, without the permit step.
How long before the transfer should we start? Allow time for the entity’s registrations and payroll set-up, plus the approval step if it falls in the first year. Starting a few months ahead is comfortable.
Is there a cost to leave the EOR? The services agreement ends with notice. We prepare the final payslip or the transfer documents as part of the service.

## Who Can Sponsor an Italian Work Permit? EOR, Own Entity or Nobody
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/who-can-sponsor-italian-work-permit-eor-entity.html
Summary: A work permit needs an employer in Italy. The options a company abroad has, how long each takes, and when an Employer of Record is the faster route.
For an ordinary hire in Italy, a company abroad has three options: an Employer of Record, its own Italian entity, or a contractor. For a non-EU professional who needs a permit, the list shrinks to two. This article explains why, and how to choose.
The rule behind it   Italian work permits for employees, the Blue Card included, are requested by the employer at the Sportello Unico per l’Immigrazione. The joint circular of the Ministry of Labour and Ministry of the Interior of 28 March 2024 explains how employers file Blue Card applications with these desks. The employer then signs the stay contract with the worker after arrival, and runs Italian payroll.
All of that presumes an employer that exists in Italy.
Option 1: your own Italian entity   You incorporate a company in Italy, typically a limited company (Srl), or register a branch. Then you open a bank account, register for tax, social security and injury insurance, and set up payroll. Only then can the entity file the permit.
When it makes sense: you plan a stable team in Italy, you need a legal presence for sales or contracts, or you already have the entity.
The downside: months of setup before the first permit can even be filed, plus fixed costs for accounting, payroll and annual filings whether you employ one person or ten.
Option 2: an Employer of Record   An EOR is an Italian company that becomes the legal employer of your person. It files the permit, signs the stay contract and the employment contract, and runs payroll. You keep directing the work.
When it makes sense: you are sponsoring one or a few people, you want them in Italy as soon as the permit allows, or you are not yet sure Italy will become a long-term base.
The cost: with ItalyBlueCard, €250 per employee per month and €2,500 per visa case, plus the actual employment cost billed monthly.
Option 3: a contractor agreement   Not an option for a permit. A contractor agreement does not support an employee work permit. And a person living in Italy and working only for you as a contractor is a reclassification risk.
Side by side   EOR Own entity Can file the permit From day one After incorporation and registrations Signs stay contract EOR Your entity Your Italian obligations None Payroll, filings, accounts Monthly cost Employment cost + €250 Employment cost + local accounting and payroll Exit End the services agreement Close or keep the company Moving from one to the other   Many companies start with an EOR and open an entity later. The employee can be transferred without losing seniority. The permit is then updated with the new employer; in the first twelve months of a Blue Card, a change of employer needs the prior approval of the labour office, which counts as given after 15 days without reply. Timing the transfer after the first year avoids that step.
A word on group transfers   If your group already has an Italian subsidiary, a transfer route for managers and specialists within a group may apply. Without one, there is nothing to transfer to, and the EOR is the practical route. See intra-company transfer .
Our recommendation   Use an EOR for the first people, and revisit the entity question when the team is stable. More in EOR, entity or contractors .
One more thing   Can a co-working membership or virtual office in Italy sponsor? No. A sponsor must be an actual employer in Italy.
Is the EOR the employer for all legal purposes? Yes, in Italy. Your company directs the work under the services agreement.
Can a relocation company sponsor? Only if it is itself the employer. Many work with an EOR for this reason. See partners .
What does the company abroad sign? One services agreement with us. The employee signs the Italian employment contract with us. The company never needs Italian registrations.
How long is the services agreement? It runs as long as the employment, and can be ended with notice. Ending it means ending or transferring the employment, which follows Italian rules.
Can we use the EOR for EU staff too? Yes. The same contract and payroll, without the visa step.

## From Contractor to Italian Employee: Why a Move to Italy Needs a Real Contract
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/contractor-to-employee-before-moving-to-italy.html
Summary: Many professionals work for a foreign company as contractors. Why that does not support an Italian work permit, and how converting to an employment contract through an EOR works.
A common story: a developer in Pune, a designer in Curitiba or an analyst in Izmir has worked for a European or American company as a contractor for years. Invoices every month, no employment contract. Now they want to move to Italy and keep the job. Can the contract simply move with them?
Usually not.
Why a contractor agreement does not work for the permit   The Blue Card and the ordinary work permit are both permits for employed work. They are requested by an employer in Italy, on the basis of an employment contract or a binding job offer of at least six months for the Blue Card. A services agreement with a foreign company is neither.
Self-employment permits exist, but they are a different route with their own conditions, and a Blue Card allows self-employment only alongside qualified employment.
Why it is also risky for the company   If a person lives in Italy and works only for one company, on its schedule, with its tools, under its direction, Italian authorities can treat the arrangement as employment. The company may then owe the contributions and taxes it should have paid, plus penalties. A long-standing contractor who moves to Italy and keeps working the same way is exactly that profile.
The conversion   The clean solution is to convert the contractor into an employee in Italy. If the company has no Italian entity, an Employer of Record becomes the employer:
Agree the salary. The gross annual salary in euros, at or above the Blue Card threshold if that is the route. Draft the contract under the right CCNL, with level, hours, probation and an IP and confidentiality clause in favour of the company. File the permit with the EOR as employer. End the contractor agreement when the employment starts, so the two do not overlap in Italy. Run payroll from the first day. How to set the salary   Contractors usually think in terms of a daily or monthly fee that covers everything. An employee’s salary is different: the employer adds about 30% in social contributions, plus INAIL and the TFR accrual. The 13th month and leave are paid too.
So the employment cost to the company is higher than the gross salary, and the employee’s net is lower than a contractor fee of the same size. Our cost calculator helps both sides find a number that works. A useful approach: start from the company’s current annual budget for the contractor, then work back to a RAL that keeps total cost close to it.
What the person gains   a work permit and residence in Italy; Italian pension contributions; public health care; at least four weeks of paid leave, paid sick leave, parental leave; the 13th month and TFR; protection against dismissal without a valid reason; a payslip that landlords and banks understand. What the company gains   no reclassification risk; no need to open an entity; one monthly invoice, €250 plus the employment cost, in EUR or USD; the IP of the work assigned by contract. Seniority   Years as a contractor do not automatically count as employment seniority in Italy. If the company wants to recognise them, it can agree a higher level or above-minimum pay, or shorten the probation.
Tell us about your contract and we will propose the switch.
Before you ask   Can I stay a contractor until the permit arrives? Yes, while you live outside Italy. The employment contract starts when you start working in Italy.
Will my net income drop? Compared with a gross contractor fee, usually yes. But you gain pension, health care, leave and severance that a contractor pays for himself.
Who owns the work I did as a contractor? That depends on your contractor agreement. The new employment contract covers work done from its start date.
Can the company keep paying my invoices from abroad after I move? No. Once you live and work in Italy, the employment contract replaces the contractor agreement. Keeping both would recreate the risk the conversion removes.
What if I also have other clients? Tell us before signing. Your employment contract may limit side work, and the Blue Card allows self-employment only alongside the qualified job, not instead of it.

## Losing Your Job on an Italian Blue Card: What Happens Next
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/losing-job-blue-card-italy-what-happens.html
Summary: Dismissal, resignation or the end of a contract: what you receive, how long you can stay, how to change employer, and what the Blue Card allows you to do.
Nobody moves to a new country expecting the job to end. But companies change plans, projects stop, managers move on. If you hold an Italian Blue Card, the law gives you more room than many people think. Here is what happens and what to do.
If the company ends your employment   Italian employment is not at-will. After probation, dismissal needs a valid reason: just cause, or a justified objective or subjective reason. The CCNL notice period applies, or pay in lieu of notice. Unfair dismissal can lead to compensation or, in some cases, reinstatement.
In your final payslip you receive:
salary for the days worked and the notice period; the accrued share of the 13th and 14th month; unused leave; the TFR severance accrued during your employment, unless it went monthly into a pension fund. If you are dismissed you may be entitled to unemployment benefit (NASpI) under the usual rules.
If you resign   You give the notice set by your CCNL. You receive the same final items except, of course, the notice pay if you do not work the notice. Resignations in Italy are filed online; we help you do it.
Your permit after the job ends   Article 27-quater gives Blue Card holders specific rights:
you may look for and take up another job while unemployed (paragraph 13-bis); in the first twelve months, a new job must still match the conditions of the card, and a change of employer requires the prior approval of the local labour office, which counts as given if it does not reply within 15 days (paragraph 13); after twelve months, you have equal access to the labour market. How long you can remain unemployed before the permit is at risk depends on the rules for your permit; we check your case at the time.
Changing employer   If you find a new job, the new employer must meet the same Blue Card conditions: salary, qualification, contract length. In the first year the labour office approval applies. If the new company has no Italian entity either, we can employ you on its behalf with a new contract.
If your original employer abroad simply wants to stop, but another company is interested in you, tell us early. A seamless switch, where the new contract starts the day after the old one ends, is the best outcome for your permit and your income.
Self-employment   The Blue Card allows self-employment alongside the qualified job. It is not a replacement for it. If you plan to become a freelancer full time, that is a different permit, and needs advice.
What to do in the first week   Ask for the termination in writing and check the dates. Ask us for your final payslip estimate. Check your permit expiry date. Update your CV and contact companies. Tell them you hold a Blue Card. If dismissed, check NASpI eligibility. If your family is with you, check how their permits depend on yours. For the company abroad   If you employ someone in Italy through us and need to end the arrangement, talk to us before telling the employee. The procedure and notice must be right, and a respectful process matters even more when someone has moved their life for the job. We handle the paperwork and explain the cost in advance.
In short   You are not left without rights. Notice, final pay, TFR, possibly NASpI, and a Blue Card that lets you look for the next job. Contact us as soon as you know.
You might also ask   Do I have to leave Italy immediately? No. Ask us what applies to your permit, and use the time to look for a new role.
Can I get my TFR if it went into a pension fund? Fund rules decide when and how you can withdraw. It is not paid out by the employer in that case.
Does unemployment affect my family’s permits? Family permits depend on your status. Keep us informed so we can check.
Can I claim NASpI if I resign? As a rule, no, except for resignation for just cause. Check the conditions before resigning.
What if my dismissal seems unfair? Italian law lets you challenge it within short deadlines. Speak to a labour lawyer or a union quickly; do not wait until your final payslip.

## Probation in Italy When You Move on a Work Visa
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/probation-period-sponsored-employee-italy.html
Summary: How the Italian probation period works, what it means for a relocated employee and their sponsor, and how to use it well on both sides.
Italian employment contracts usually start with a probation period, the periodo di prova. During probation either side can end the contract without notice and without giving a reason. After it, the job becomes much more stable. For someone who has crossed continents for the job, probation deserves some thought.
The basics   Probation must be written in the contract before work starts; otherwise it does not apply. Its length is set by the CCNL, by job level, up to six months for most roles. During probation, either side can end the relationship freely. After probation, the employee is confirmed automatically. Ending the job then requires a valid reason and the CCNL notice, or the employee’s resignation. Why it feels different when you relocated   For a local hire, a failed probation is a setback. For a relocated employee, it can be much more: a lease signed, children enrolled in school, a permit tied to the job. Two things soften that risk.
First, the permit does not disappear overnight. As a Blue Card holder you can look for another job while unemployed, and the permit’s validity is linked to the contract terms. We tell you exactly what applies in your case.
Second, probation is mostly a period to check fit, not a trap. Most professionals who relocate already know the company, often they already work for it. The probation then is a formality that the Italian contract needs, not a real test.
Advice for the company employing you   Set clear goals for the probation. Write them down and share them in the first week. Do not leave the review to the last day. Hold a mid-probation conversation. If something is wrong, say so early. Remember the family. If the employee’s family is joining, a decision late in probation affects several people. Be honest early. Do not use probation as a substitute for planning. If the role is uncertain, consider a fixed-term contract instead, so expectations are clear. Advice for you   Ask in advance what the probation goals are and who decides. Keep notes of the work you deliver in the first months. Do not over-commit financially in the first weeks: a temporary flat and a modest budget until probation ends is sensible. Plan the family move with the probation date in mind, unless you already know the company well. Probation and the permit timeline   Probation starts on your first working day in Italy, not on the date of the offer. If the consulate step takes longer than expected, probation simply starts later. Work done for the company from your home country before the move, under a different contract, does not count towards Italian probation.
When probation ends without confirmation   The contract ends. You receive pay for the days worked, accrued 13th month, unused leave and the TFR accrued so far. As your employer we file the termination and tell you what it means for your permit and your options.
When probation is passed   Nothing needs to happen: you are confirmed automatically. From then on, the Italian rules on dismissal apply. If the company later decides to end the arrangement, it needs a valid reason, and the CCNL notice applies.
A note on prior service   If you have already worked for the company abroad for years, ask whether the probation can be shortened or waived. It is a reasonable request, and it signals the company’s commitment.
Read more about contracts, leave and termination , or talk to us before you sign.
Last questions   Can probation be extended? Only within the CCNL limits and in specific cases such as long absences. It cannot be extended at will.
Do I accrue leave during probation? Yes, leave, 13th month and TFR all accrue from day one.
Is probation shorter for junior roles? Usually, yes. The CCNL sets lengths by level, with shorter periods for lower levels.
Can I resign during probation? Yes, without notice, like the employer. If you do, think about the permit first and talk to us.
Does probation affect the permit application? No. The permit is based on the contract, which includes probation as a normal clause. Probation starts only when you start work in Italy.
Is probation the same for EU colleagues? Yes. The CCNL applies to everyone at your level, whatever their nationality.

## Permanent or Fixed-Term Contract: What It Changes for Your Italian Permit
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/permanent-vs-fixed-term-contract-permit-length.html
Summary: A permanent contract gives a two-year Blue Card; a fixed-term one gives the contract length plus three months. How contract type affects permit, renewal and planning.
When a company abroad hires you through an Employer of Record, one of the first choices is the contract type: permanent (a tempo indeterminato) or fixed-term (a tempo determinato). In Italy both are common. For a sponsored employee, the choice also shapes the permit.
The rule for the Blue Card   Article 27-quater, paragraph 11 is clear:
with a permanent contract, the Blue Card residence permit lasts two years; with any other contract, it lasts the length of the employment relationship plus three months. And paragraph 5 sets a floor: the contract or binding offer must last at least six months.
So a twelve-month fixed-term contract gives a permit of about fifteen months, and a renewal tied to a contract extension. A permanent contract gives two years, renewable while the job continues.
Why companies choose fixed-term   Companies abroad sometimes prefer fixed-term because they are testing a market or a project, or because they are used to at-will employment and see a fixed end date as a safety valve. In Italy, fixed-term contracts have legal limits on total duration and on renewals.
From the permit side, a fixed-term contract means:
shorter permit, earlier renewal; a renewal that depends on the contract being extended or converted; less certainty for a lease, a loan or a family reunification file. Why we usually suggest permanent   A permanent Italian contract is not a life sentence. It includes a probation period, up to six months depending on the CCNL, during which either side can end it without notice. After probation, ending it needs a valid reason and the CCNL notice period, like any employment in Italy.
In exchange, the employee gets a two-year permit, a stronger position with landlords, and a simpler family file. For a company that is serious about the person, it is usually the better choice.
Part-time   Part-time contracts are possible and standard in Italy. For the Blue Card, what counts is the salary actually paid, so a part-time contract must still reach the threshold on its own. Few qualified roles do; plan for full time.
Converting later   A fixed-term contract can be converted into a permanent one. The permit is then renewed on the new terms. If you plan to convert, do it before the permit renewal so the renewal can use the permanent contract.
What happens at the end of a fixed-term contract   If the contract ends and is not renewed, you receive your final pay, TFR and unused leave. Your permit lasts three months beyond the contract. As a Blue Card holder you may look for another job during unemployment. Talk to us well before the end date: a new employer, or the same company through us on a new contract, needs time to arrange.
A short comparison   Permanent Fixed-term Blue Card permit 2 years Contract length + 3 months Minimum length for Blue Card - 6 months Ends with Notice and a valid reason, or resignation The end date, or earlier for just cause Landlords and banks Strong Weaker Family file Simpler Tied to contract length Our advice   If the company employing you expects the role to last, choose permanent with a well-used probation period. If it genuinely is a project, choose a fixed term long enough to be worth the move, and agree in advance what happens at the end. Read the contract behind the permit or ask us .
Doubts we clear up   Can a fixed-term contract be renewed indefinitely? No. Italian law limits duration and renewals of fixed-term contracts. We check the plan against the limits.
Does a permanent contract cost the employer more? The monthly cost is the same. The difference is in how and when the relationship can end.
Which is better for a mortgage? Banks strongly prefer permanent contracts that have passed probation.
Can I resign from a permanent contract? Yes, at any time, giving the notice set by your CCNL. A permanent contract binds the employer far more than the employee.
Does the contract type change my salary or benefits? No. Pay, leave, 13th month and TFR are the same; fixed-term employees have the same rights for the duration of the contract.
What if the company is unsure about Italy long term? A permanent contract with an EOR is still easy to end correctly if plans change, with notice and a valid reason. The company does not take on an entity it may later need to close.

## Why Your Collective Agreement (CCNL) Matters for Your Permit
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/ccnl-collective-agreement-visa-salary.html
Summary: The CCNL sets the minimum salary for your level, your hours, leave and notice. For a sponsored employee it is also part of the salary test. What to check.
Almost every employee in Italy works under a national collective agreement, a CCNL (contratto collettivo nazionale di lavoro). It is negotiated by unions and employers’ associations for a sector, and it sets most of the rules of your job. For a non-EU professional, it also plays a direct role in the permit.
What a CCNL sets   Job levels and the minimum salary for each level; working hours and overtime rates; leave, including extra paid hours off (ROL) on top of the four statutory weeks; probation length; notice periods, by level and seniority; the number of installments, 13 or 14; sick pay top-ups, supplementary health funds and other benefits. Your contract states which CCNL applies and your level. Individual terms can be better than the CCNL, never worse.
The CCNL and the Blue Card   Article 27-quater sets a double salary test for the Blue Card: the salary must be at least the level set by the national collective agreements, and at least the ISTAT average gross annual salary. Usually the second figure is the higher one for qualified roles, but the first still applies: an offer that reaches the ISTAT figure but sits below the CCNL minimum for your level is not acceptable.
That is why the level matters. A senior engineer placed at a junior level might pass the ISTAT test but be underpaid against the agreement, and the mismatch between qualification and level can raise questions in the file.
Which CCNL applies   It is not a free choice. It follows the sector of the employer’s activity and the type of work. Two common ones for professionals:
Commerce and services (Terziario, Distribuzione e Servizi): offices, IT services, consulting, sales. 14 installments. Metalworking industry (Metalmeccanico): engineering, production, technical roles. 13 installments. The employer’s social contribution rate and the injury insurance rate also depend on sector and role, so the CCNL affects the total cost too. Our cost calculator compares the two.
What to check in your contract   CCNL name. Is it a national agreement signed by the main unions? Level. Does it match your qualification and role? Ask for the job description of the level. Minimum vs your salary. Your salary should be at or above the minimum for the level, and above the Blue Card threshold. Installments. 13 or 14? Probation and notice. How long, and how they apply to you. Extra benefits. Supplementary health fund, pension fund, meal vouchers. When the CCNL changes   CCNLs are renewed periodically, usually with salary increases. The increases apply automatically. If your salary is right at the minimum, the renewal raises it; if you are above, the increase may be absorbed into your above-minimum pay, depending on your contract.
Why it is good news   For someone arriving in a new country, the CCNL is a safety net. Your minimum pay, hours and leave are not negotiated case by case; they are written down and apply to everyone at your level. Disputes are rare when everyone reads the same document.
Our part   As your Employer of Record we choose the CCNL from the job and the activity of the company employing you, explain the choice in the quote, and check the salary against both the CCNL and the Blue Card threshold before filing. Read more in the contract behind the permit .
Short answers to common doubts   Can I choose a CCNL with a lower cost? No. The CCNL follows the activity and the job. Picking one only for cost is a compliance risk.
Do I need to join a union? No. The CCNL applies whether you are a member or not.
Where can I read my CCNL? CCNL texts are published by the signing parties and collected by public bodies. We send you the relevant chapters with your contract.
Is the CCNL in English? The official text is in Italian. We summarise the parts that matter to you in English, and the contract itself is bilingual.
What if the company abroad has its own handbook? Company policies can add to the CCNL, never reduce it. A generous global leave policy can apply on top of the Italian minimum, for example. We check any handbook against the CCNL before you start.
Does the CCNL decide my job title? It decides your level and its description. Your job title in the company can be different; what matters for the permit is that role, level and qualification are consistent.
