## The 13th and 14th Month: Extra Salaries and Your Relocation Budget
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/thirteenth-fourteenth-month-pay-relocation.html
Summary: How Italy's 13th and 14th month salaries work, why they matter in your first year after moving, and how employers abroad can spread them evenly.
If you come from a country where a salary is twelve equal monthly payments, Italy has a surprise for you, mostly a pleasant one. Salaries here are paid in 13 installments, sometimes 14. The extra installments are the tredicesima (13th month) and the quattordicesima (14th month).
What they are   The 13th month is mandatory under every national collective agreement and is paid in December. The 14th month is paid only where the CCNL provides it, such as Commerce and services, usually in June or July.
They are not bonuses. They are part of your annual gross salary, the RAL. If your RAL is split into 13 installments, each monthly payslip carries one thirteenth, and December carries two.
Why it matters in year one   Two effects for people relocating.
Your first months are leaner. A RAL paid in 14 installments gives smaller monthly payslips than the same RAL in 12. Deposits, agency fees and furniture all fall in those first months. Budget the move on the monthly installment, not on the RAL divided by twelve.
Your first December is partial. The 13th month accrues month by month. If you start in September, your December extra installment covers about four months, not twelve. The same applies to the 14th month in summer.
How the threshold sees them   For the Blue Card, the salary is checked as an annual gross figure. The 13th and 14th month are part of it. Ask for the RAL, not the monthly figure, when comparing your offer with the threshold.
Spreading them evenly   Some employers abroad prefer twelve equal invoices, and some employees prefer twelve equal payslips. Where the CCNL or an individual agreement allows it, the 13th and 14th month can be paid pro rata in each monthly payslip. The annual amount stays the same.
At ItalyBlueCard we spread the 13th and 14th month pro rata over the monthly invoices by default, so the company employing you sees a flat cost and no December spike. Whether your payslip is also spread depends on the agreement; we explain the options before you sign.
When you leave   If you leave mid-year, the accrued part of the 13th and 14th month is paid in your final payslip, together with unused leave and the TFR. Nothing is lost.
Taxes and contributions   The extra installments are taxed and carry contributions like normal salary. The December payslip is often larger than expected, but with a progressive tax it is also taxed more heavily that month; the year-end adjustment evens it out.
A worked view without numbers   Imagine two offers with the same RAL. One is under a CCNL with 13 installments, the other with 14. The annual gross pay is identical, the annual cost to the employer is identical. Only the timing differs: the 14-installment contract pays less each month and more in July and December.
Use the net pay calculator and switch between 12, 13 and 14 installments to see the difference for your RAL.
For the company employing you   The extra months are part of the cost, not an extra. Our cost calculator shows the full monthly invoice, with the 13th and 14th month spread and TFR paid monthly into the employee’s chosen fund, so no year-end liabilities build up.
Checklist   Ask for the RAL and the number of installments Budget the move on the monthly installment Expect a partial December in year one Agree whether the extra months are spread Check the final payslip includes accruals if you leave Odds and ends   Is the 13th month guaranteed? Yes, under every CCNL. It is not discretionary.
Do part-time employees get it? Yes, pro rata to the hours worked.
Is the 13th month affected by sick leave? Rules depend on the CCNL; periods of paid sickness usually still accrue it. We apply the CCNL rule in payroll.
Is it paid during probation? Yes. It accrues from the first day of employment, and if probation ends without confirmation the accrued part is paid in the final payslip.
Can I ask for the 13th month in advance to pay my deposit? Advances are possible by agreement with the employer. Ask the company employing you; we process it in payroll as an advance on the accrued amount.
How does it show on the payslip? As a separate line, tredicesima mensilità, with its own tax and contribution calculation. If spread monthly, a smaller pro rata line appears every month instead.

## Your First Italian Payslip: How Gross Becomes Net
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/italian-net-pay-explained-newcomers.html
Summary: Employee social security, IRPEF bands, employment tax credits and local surcharges, explained for professionals who just moved to Italy.
The first Italian payslip, the busta paga, is a dense page of codes and abbreviations. For someone who just arrived it can be alarming: the gap between gross and net looks large, and the line items have unfamiliar names. Here is how to read it.
Step 1: employee social security   From gross pay, the employer first withholds your share of social security: 9.19% for most private-sector employees, plus 1% on the part of your annual pay above €56,224. These contributions go to INPS and build your Italian pension. They also fund unemployment benefit, sick pay and maternity pay.
For people first insured from 1996 onwards, which includes anyone starting an Italian career now, pension contributions stop above an annual ceiling of €122,295 in 2026.
Step 2: income tax (IRPEF)   What remains is taxable income. Income tax, IRPEF, is progressive:
Taxable income Rate Up to €28,000 23% €28,000 to €50,000 33% Above €50,000 43% Each band is taxed at its own rate: moving into a higher band only affects the part above the limit.
Step 3: tax credits   Employment tax credits reduce the tax. They are largest on lower salaries and reach zero at €50,000. Between €20,000 and €40,000 an additional credit of up to €1,000 applies. Credits for dependent family members can reduce tax further once your spouse or children are with you and registered.
Step 4: local surcharges   On top of IRPEF you pay a regional and a municipal surcharge, depending on where you live. Rates and exemption thresholds vary by city; Milan, for instance, exempts incomes up to €23,000 from its 0.8% municipal surcharge, according to secondary sources. The surcharges are often withheld in installments during the following year, so your first months may look slightly better than your steady state.
What the payslip shows   A typical payslip lists:
Competenze: what you earned, base pay, any above-minimum amount, overtime, allowances, the 13th or 14th month when due; Trattenute: what was withheld, contributions, IRPEF, surcharges; Netto in busta: what is transferred to your account; Progressivi: year-to-date totals; TFR: the severance accrued, which is not paid out monthly but set aside or sent to a pension fund. Why your first payslip may look different   You joined mid-month, so the salary is pro rata. The 13th month accrues month by month; if you joined in, say, September, December’s extra installment is only partial. Tax credits are spread over the year and adjusted at year end. Your family is not yet registered for dependent credits. The CU at year end   Each year you receive the Certificazione Unica (CU), the annual summary of income, tax and contributions, by 16 March. It is your proof of income for leases, loans, and for a family reunification file. Keep every one.
Try your own numbers   The net pay calculator applies these 2026 rules to your RAL and city. It is an estimate for a single person with no other income; your real payslip may differ slightly.
Who to ask   When something on your payslip looks wrong, ask the person who calculated it. As your employer we run payroll in-house and answer in Italian or English. Read more in from RAL to net pay .
Questions from employers and staff   Why is my December payslip larger? The 13th month is paid in December, unless it is spread pro rata.
Can I reduce my tax? Through deductions for some expenses in your annual return, and through tax-efficient benefits such as meal vouchers and pension fund contributions.
What is the trattamento integrativo on my payslip? A tax supplement for lower incomes. Most professionals on Blue Card salaries are above the range where it applies.
What are the codes on the right of the payslip? Year-to-date totals and the details of tax and contribution bases. We go through them with you on your first payslip, line by line, in English if you prefer.
Is there a special regime for people moving to Italy? Italy has had tax incentives for workers who move their tax residence to Italy, with conditions that have changed over time. We have not verified the current rules for this article; ask an adviser whether they apply to you before you move.
Will my net pay change when my family arrives? It can: credits for dependent family members reduce IRPEF once your spouse or children are registered as dependants. Tell us when they arrive.

## Reading an Italian Offer: RAL, Installments and the Blue Card Threshold
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/ral-gross-salary-blue-card-threshold.html
Summary: Italian offers state the RAL, the annual gross salary. Why it is the figure that counts for the Blue Card, what is not included in it, and how to compare it with an offer from home.
An Italian offer letter usually leads with three letters: RAL, retribuzione annua lorda, the annual gross salary. For a professional moving on a Blue Card, the RAL is more than a number to negotiate. It is the figure the immigration desk compares with the salary threshold. Getting it right protects both your permit and your budget.
What the RAL includes   The RAL is the total gross salary for a year of full-time work, before the employee’s contributions and income tax are withheld. It includes:
the base salary for your job level under the collective agreement (CCNL); any amount agreed above the minimum (superminimo); the 13th month and, where the CCNL provides it, the 14th month. It does not include:
the employer’s social contributions to INPS and INAIL; the TFR severance accrual (6.91% of pay, set aside every year); variable pay, bonuses and commissions not guaranteed in the contract; meal vouchers, fringe benefits and reimbursements. Why it matters for the Blue Card   Article 27-quater requires a salary at least equal to the level of the applicable CCNL and to the average gross annual salary published by ISTAT. A secondary source reports the figure at about €36,300 a year; we will update this when we read the official notice.
In practice:
Use gross, not net. A net figure quoted from your home country’s habits is not comparable. Use guaranteed pay. A target bonus does not help you reach the threshold. Use the annual figure. A monthly gross multiplied by twelve misses the 13th and 14th installments; a monthly figure multiplied by fourteen may overstate it if the CCNL pays only thirteen. Part-time counts pro rata. A part-time contract is measured on what it actually pays. Installments   The RAL is paid in 13 installments, or 14 under some CCNLs such as Commerce and services. The 13th comes in December, the 14th in June or July. Some companies agree to spread them evenly over twelve months; the annual amount is the same.
For relocation this matters: your first months’ cash flow is lower than a twelve-installment salary suggests, just when deposits and furniture are due. Plan for it.
Comparing with an offer from home   The honest comparison is net with net, with the cost of living on top. Use the net pay calculator with your RAL and city. Then add what Italy includes that you may be paying for at home: public health care, pension contributions, a minimum of four weeks of paid leave, TFR at the end of the job.
From the employer’s side, the comparison is total cost with total cost. The employer adds about 30% in contributions, INAIL and TFR on top of the RAL. Our cost calculator shows the month-by-month figure, including our €250 monthly fee.
Negotiating with the threshold in mind   If your offer is close to the threshold, a small increase in guaranteed pay can move your case from the quota route to the Blue Card, which has no quota and a 30-day deadline for the work authorisation. Ask the company to consider it before filing, not after. Converting a planned bonus into guaranteed pay is one way to do it.
Raises later on   Once you are in Italy, raises go into a written amendment to the contract. A pay cut that took you below the threshold could expose the permit, so talk to us before any change of salary or role, especially in the first twelve months.
Summary   Ask for the RAL in euros, check what it includes, compare it with the threshold on guaranteed gross pay, and plan your first months’ cash flow around the installments. Send us the offer if you want a check.
Worth asking   Is the RAL the same as a “CTC” or “package”? No. A cost-to-company figure includes employer costs. The RAL is the employee’s gross salary only.
Can a signing bonus help reach the threshold? A one-off bonus is not guaranteed annual pay. Rely on the fixed salary.
Should I ask for the salary in euros? Yes. The Italian contract is in euros; the company can budget in its own currency, and our invoice can be in USD at the EUR reference rate.
What if my offer is exactly at the threshold? Leave a margin. CCNL renewals and ISTAT updates move the reference figures over time, and a renewal is checked against the rules in force at that moment.
Does overtime count? Overtime is variable and not guaranteed, so it does not help reach the threshold. Plan on fixed pay.

## Working in Italy for a Company Abroad: Questions Professionals Ask
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/working-from-italy-for-a-foreign-company-faq.html
Summary: You want to live in Italy and keep working for a company in another country. How an Employer of Record makes it legal, and what it means for your contract, pay and permit.
A growing share of the people who contact us are not looking for an Italian job. They already have a job, with a company in India, Brazil, the US, Turkey or elsewhere, and they want to do it from Italy. Maybe a partner lives here, maybe they fell for a city, maybe the company wants someone close to European customers.
This is possible and common. It needs a structure, though. Here are the questions we hear most.
Can I just move and keep working remotely?   Not for long, and not as a non-EU national. To work in Italy you need a permit that allows work. A tourist entry does not. Working from Italy for months also creates income tax and social security obligations, and can expose your company to having a taxable presence in Italy.
Why can my company not sponsor me directly?   The work authorisation is requested by an employer in Italy. A company with no Italian entity cannot easily file it, and opening an entity just for you takes months and creates ongoing costs.
What is an Employer of Record, from my side?   A company in Italy that becomes your legal employer. It signs an Italian employment contract with you, files your permit, pays your salary and withholds tax and contributions. Your company abroad pays the EOR a monthly fee plus your employment cost, and keeps directing your work: your manager, your team, your tasks stay the same.
With ItalyBlueCard the fee is €250 per month, invoiced in EUR or USD at the EUR reference rate.
Which permit would I get?   Usually the EU Blue Card : a degree or qualifying experience, a contract of at least six months, and a salary at or above the threshold (reported at about €36,300 gross a year). Otherwise a quota work permit.
Will my salary stay the same?   The company decides the salary, but it will be expressed as an Italian gross annual salary (RAL) in euros, paid in 13 or 14 installments. Your net pay depends on Italian tax and contributions. Try the net pay calculator before you agree a number.
Do I lose my benefits?   Some change shape. You gain Italian ones: INPS pension contributions, public health care, at least four weeks of paid leave, the 13th month and TFR severance. Benefits from home, such as a stock plan, may continue; their tax treatment in Italy depends on the plan and should be checked.
What happens to my pension at home?   Contributions in Italy build an Italian pension. Whether periods can be combined with your home country depends on social security agreements between the two countries. Ask an adviser in your home country.
Can I work for other clients too?   A Blue Card allows self-employment alongside the qualified job. Your employment contract will also have confidentiality and IP clauses in favour of your company; check before taking side work.
What if the company stops the arrangement?   Then Italian rules on dismissal and notice apply, as for any employee. As a Blue Card holder you can look for another job while unemployed. You receive TFR, unused leave and the accrued 13th month in your final payslip.
How do I convince my manager?   Send them this page and the cost calculator . Most companies worry about legal exposure and cost. An EOR removes the first and makes the second predictable.
Questions worth a minute   Can I keep my home employment contract too? Two parallel employment contracts for the same work create tax and social security problems. Usually the home contract is suspended or ended while you are employed in Italy.
Who sets my working hours? Your company, within the limits of the Italian contract and CCNL: normal week of 40 hours, average including overtime of no more than 48.
Can I work from home in Italy? Yes. The remote work agreement (lavoro agile) is written into your contract.
Does my company need an Italian bank account? No. The company pays our invoice from its own account, in EUR or USD.
Will I appear on my company’s org chart? That is up to the company. Legally we are your employer in Italy; in practice you are a member of their team, with their tools, their email and their manager. Most people we employ are indistinguishable from colleagues in other countries.
How quickly can we start? As soon as the permit allows. The Blue Card nulla osta has a 30-day legal deadline; documents and the consulate add time. See planning a start date .

## Health Care in Italy for Newcomers on a Work Permit
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/italian-national-health-service-newcomers-work-permit.html
Summary: How non-EU employees enrol in the Italian national health service, choose a family doctor, what the employer pays and what supplementary health funds add.
People moving from countries where health insurance is tied to the employer often ask the same thing: “Which insurance will the company give me in Italy?”. The short answer is that in Italy, your health care does not depend on your employer. As a resident employee you enrol in the national health service, the Servizio Sanitario Nazionale (SSN), funded by general taxation.
Enrolment   Enrolment is done at the local health authority (ASL) for the area where you live. Bring your passport, residence permit or permit receipt, tax code and, usually, your employment contract or proof of address. Family members who join you enrol in the same way.
At enrolment you choose a medico di base, a family doctor, from a list of available doctors in your area. For children there are paediatricians. You then receive a health card that also shows your tax code.
The exact documents and procedure vary by region. Check the ASL website or ask us before you go.
What it covers   The SSN covers general practitioner visits, hospital care, emergency care and specialist care on referral, with a co-payment (ticket) for some services and medicines. Waiting times for non-urgent specialist visits can be long in some areas, and many people use private clinics for faster appointments, paying out of pocket or through a supplementary fund.
What the employer pays   Nothing directly for the public system. Health care is not an employer cost in Italy, and it does not appear on the invoice we send to the company employing you. The employer’s social contributions to INPS fund pensions, unemployment, sickness pay and maternity, not the health service.
Some collective agreements (CCNLs) include a supplementary health fund. Contributions are paid by the employer and are exempt from tax up to €3,615.20 a year. These funds reimburse private visits, dental care and other services. If your CCNL has one, you are enrolled automatically.
Sick leave is separate   Health care and sick pay are two different things. When you are ill, your doctor sends a medical certificate online to INPS. Your pay during sickness is shared between INPS and the employer according to the CCNL. Your job is protected for a period set by the CCNL.
The first weeks   There can be a short gap between landing and completing enrolment. Some people keep travel or private cover for the first weeks; others are covered from the date the permit application is filed. Check your situation with us before you travel.
Bring:
a summary of your medical history, ideally translated; current prescriptions with the active ingredient, not just the brand name; vaccination records for children, which schools ask for. Private insurance: needed or not?   For most employees, not needed. It can still make sense if you want faster specialist access or cover in other countries. If the company employing you wants to offer it as a benefit, we can include it in payroll; contributions to qualifying health funds have the tax treatment described above.
Questions we often hear   Does my spouse need to be employed to get health care? No. Family members who join you with a family permit enrol in the health service too.
Can I keep my doctor from home? You can keep seeing them privately when you travel back, but in Italy you need an Italian family doctor for referrals and prescriptions.
Does the Blue Card change anything? No. Blue Card holders enrol like other residents with a work permit.
More on the first weeks in relocation .
Things candidates ask   Is enrolment automatic? No. You enrol at the ASL with your documents. We tell you which office covers your address.
Are dental care and glasses covered? Coverage is limited. Supplementary health funds, where the CCNL has one, often reimburse part of these costs.
What about emergencies before enrolment? Emergency care is provided in any case. Keep travel insurance for the first weeks until enrolment is complete.
Do I pay anything for the health card? Enrolment for employees with a work permit is part of the public system funded by taxation; check with the ASL whether any local administrative step applies.
Can I see a specialist directly? Usually you need a referral from your family doctor for public specialist care. Private specialists can be seen directly, at your own cost or through a supplementary fund.

## The Codice Fiscale: Your Italian Tax Code Before and After Arrival
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/codice-fiscale-italian-tax-code-newcomers.html
Summary: What the Italian tax code is, why your contract, payroll, lease and bank all need it, and how newcomers on a work visa get one.
Every newcomer to Italy learns the phrase codice fiscale in the first week. It is a 16-character code that identifies you to the tax agency, and it is required for almost everything: your employment contract, payroll, health service enrolment, a lease, a bank account, often even a phone contract.
What it is   The codice fiscale is issued by the Agenzia delle Entrate, the Italian tax agency. It is derived from your name, date and place of birth and sex. It does not change, and it does not by itself mean you are tax resident in Italy.
The code is printed on a card or paper certificate, and later on your health card.
When you get it   There are three common moments:
Before arrival, through the Italian consulate in your country, which can request the code for people who need it. At the immigration desk, during the permit process, where the code is often assigned. At a tax agency office in Italy, with your passport and visa. Ask your employer which applies in your case. If you already have a code from a previous stay or study in Italy, it stays valid: do not request a new one.
Why payroll needs it on day one   Your employer must notify your hire to the authorities electronically before you start work, and the notification needs your tax code. The same code is used for every monthly payroll filing, for your INPS contributions and for the annual CU tax certificate. Without it, the hire cannot be filed properly.
That is why, as your Employer of Record, we ask for the code early, and help you obtain it if it is missing.
Common problems   Name spelling. Names transliterated from other scripts, or long names with several parts, can be recorded differently on the passport, the visa and the code. A mismatch causes problems at the bank and the Questura. Check it the day you receive the code. Duplicates. People who requested a code at a consulate and again in Italy sometimes end up with two. Only one is valid; the tax agency can fix it. Family members. Each family member needs their own code, children included. Request them when the family file starts. The code and your tax position   Having a codice fiscale does not make you tax resident. Tax residence depends on where you live and register, and for how long. As an employee, income tax is withheld through payroll, so most people never file anything themselves. You receive the CU certificate every year, and you file a return only if you have other income or want to claim deductions. If you have income or assets in your home country, ask an adviser about the interaction between the two systems.
The health card   Once you enrol in the national health service, you receive a health card that also carries your codice fiscale. It is the card you show at pharmacies and doctors.
Quick checklist   Code requested or confirmed before the stay contract Spelling identical to the passport Code sent to your employer for the hire notification Codes requested for each family member Health card received after enrolment See the full relocation steps , or ask us where to request your code.
A few quick clarifications   Is the codice fiscale the same as a tax return number? It is your general identifier for all tax and many administrative purposes, used on every filing.
Can I get it online? Some consulates and the tax agency offer remote procedures. Ask us which channel is fastest from your country.
Do I need it to sign the employment contract? Yes, the hire notification and the payroll set-up both use it, so it should be ready before your first working day.
What if I lose the card? The code stays the same. You can request a duplicate certificate from the tax agency, and the code also appears on your health card once you enrol.
Is it secret? No. It appears on contracts, payslips, invoices and medical prescriptions. Treat it like a name and date of birth: not confidential, but no reason to publish it.
Does my employer abroad need it? The company abroad does not. We use it as your Italian employer for every payroll and tax filing.

## Renting a Home in Italy as a Newcomer: Leases, Deposits and the Documents You Need
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/housing-italy-newcomers-lease-documents.html
Summary: How renting works in Italy for non-EU professionals: temporary first, long lease second, what landlords ask for, and how the lease supports residence and family files.
Housing is the part of the move that worries people most, and for good reason. Italian landlords often prefer tenants with an Italian payslip and an Italian guarantor, and in the big cities good flats go quickly. With a little planning it is manageable. Here is how we suggest newcomers approach it.
Two steps, not one   Very few people sign their final lease from abroad. The usual pattern is:
Temporary accommodation for the first weeks: a serviced apartment, a furnished flat on a short contract, or a residence. It gives you an address for the consulate, the stay contract and the first appointments. A long-term lease once you know the city, the commute and the neighbourhood. This is the address you register at the municipal registry and, if your family is joining, the one checked for reunification. Book the first before the visa appointment; consulates ask for proof of accommodation, such as a lease, a hotel booking or a hosting declaration.
What a landlord will ask   your passport and permit or permit receipt; your tax code; your employment contract; recent payslips, or a letter from the employer confirming salary and start date; sometimes a guarantor or a larger deposit. The employment contract is your strongest asset. A permanent Italian contract with a known employer reassures landlords far more than an offer from a foreign company. When we are your employer, we issue the contract and an employer letter as soon as the permit is granted, and payslips from the first month.
Lease types in brief   Italian leases come in a few standard forms: long open-market leases, “agreed rent” leases with terms set by local agreements, and transitional leases for temporary needs. Each has its own minimum duration and notice rules. Read the termination clause carefully, especially if your contract or your plans may change. We do not quote durations here; ask the agent or a local adviser for the current rules of the lease you are offered.
Deposits and agency fees   Expect a security deposit and, if you use an agency, an agency fee. Both can be significant. Ask your employer whether the relocation package covers them, or whether an advance can be arranged. Housing paid or reimbursed by the employer is common in relocation packages; its tax treatment depends on how it is structured, so agree it in writing.
Housing and the family file   If your spouse or children will join you, the home must meet health and hygiene standards and be suitable for the number of occupants. The municipality checks it as part of the reunification process. A one-bedroom flat that suits you alone may not pass for a family of four.
Choose the long-term home with the final household in mind, and keep the lease, the floor plan and any certificates the agent can provide.
Where to look   Large listing portals and local agencies for the open market. Company housing lists or colleagues, often the fastest route. University cities have many furnished flats, but competition with students peaks before the academic year. Commuter towns: many people working in the big cities live outside them and commute by train, with lower rents and larger homes. Red flags   A landlord who refuses a written lease or asks to be paid in cash. A lease that cannot be registered: you need a registered lease for residence registration and for the family file. Deposits requested before you have seen the flat or met the owner or agent. Our part   As your employer we provide the documents landlords ask for. Through our relocation service we can also run the search, shortlist flats and come to viewings, quoted per case. See relocation or ask for a quote .
Small print, plain answers   Can I sign a lease before I arrive? It is possible, but risky without seeing the flat. A short temporary stay first is safer.
Will a landlord accept a foreign employer? Many prefer an Italian employer. An Italian contract and payslips from us solve that.
Can my employer be the tenant? Companies sometimes rent flats for staff. It changes the tax treatment and the residence registration. Discuss it with us before agreeing.
How long does a search take? In the big cities, good flats go quickly, and landlords often decide within days. Have your documents ready in a folder before you start viewing, so you can make an offer on the spot.
Is furnished or unfurnished better? Furnished flats are easier for the first year, especially in Milan and university cities. Unfurnished flats can be cheaper for longer stays, but you will need to buy kitchen appliances in some cases.

## The Relocation Checklist for Moving to Italy on a Work Visa
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/relocation-checklist-moving-to-italy-work-visa.html
Summary: Ninety days before, thirty days before, the first week and the first month: a practical checklist for non-EU professionals relocating to Italy with an Italian employer.
A move to Italy has two tracks running in parallel: the permit track, which your employer leads, and the life track, which is yours. People who keep both moving arrive calmer and start work sooner. This checklist is organised by time, so you can tick it off as you go.
Ninety days before   Confirm the route. Blue Card or quota permit. Read visa routes and ask the employer for the gross annual salary in euros. Confirm the employer in Italy. If the company has no Italian entity, an Employer of Record will sign your contract and sponsor the permit. Send the company this page . Order documents. Degree certificates, transcripts, experience letters, marriage and birth certificates. Ask for legalisation or apostille and plan certified Italian translations. For degrees, consider a CIMEA comparability statement. Check your passport. Validity and blank pages. Consulates have their own rules; the Embassy in Beijing, for instance, asks for a passport issued less than ten years ago with at least two blank pages. Talk to your family. Decide whether they come with you or follow. If they follow, start their documents now too. Sixty days before   Contract review. Read the Italian contract: role, level, CCNL, salary, hours, probation, notice. Ask about anything that is unclear. The salary written here is the one the permit relies on. Budget the first month. Deposit and first rent, temporary accommodation, travel, appointments. Rental deposits in Italy can be several months of rent; ask your employer about relocation support. Think about the city. Commute, schools, cost of living. See choosing a city . Thirty days before   Consular appointment. As soon as the nulla osta is issued, book the visa appointment. The nulla osta has a limited life for the visa application. Temporary housing. Book a furnished flat or residence for the first weeks. Keep the booking confirmation: consulates ask for proof of accommodation. Banking at home. Tell your bank you are moving, keep one home account open, and check card fees abroad. Health. Bring prescriptions and a summary of any ongoing treatment, translated if possible, for your new family doctor. The first week in Italy   Sign the stay contract with your employer at the immigration desk. Submit the residence permit application and keep the receipt. Get or confirm your tax code. Give your employer your Italian address and phone number. Open an Italian or EU bank account for your salary. Our first-weeks guide explains each step.
The first month   Attend the Questura appointment for fingerprints. Sign a long-term lease and register your residence at the municipal registry. Enrol in the national health service and choose a family doctor. Check your first payslip: gross pay, contributions, tax, net pay. We walk you through it. If your family is following, start the reunification file once housing is in place. Things people forget   A local SIM card early on: Italian offices often call or text. Copies of every document, on paper and in a cloud folder. The expiry date of the permit in your calendar. Driving: check whether and for how long your licence is valid in Italy, and when you need to convert it. Your home-country tax position after you leave; ask an adviser there. The role of your employer   As your Italian employer we lead the permit track, sign the stay contract, set up payroll and track the permit renewal. We can also take on the life track through our relocation service: tax code, housing search, health service and bank account, quoted per case.
Ask us for a relocation plan with dates for your case.
Edge cases   Do I need an international driving permit? Rules depend on your licence and country. Check before you arrive, and do not drive on an expired entitlement.
Should I ship furniture? Most people ship personal items and buy furniture locally. Furnished flats are common in big cities.
When should my family arrive? Usually after you have a long-term lease and the reunification conditions are met. Read bringing your family to Italy .
What should I keep in my carry-on? Passport with visa, nulla osta copy, degree and civil certificates with translations, the employment contract, the accommodation booking and any medical prescriptions. These are the documents the first appointments ask for.
Who pays for what? Agree it with the company employing you before you book anything. Flights, temporary housing and document costs are common relocation items; see building a relocation package .

## Bringing Your Family to Italy: Income, Housing and the Blue Card Advantage
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/family-reunification-italy-income-housing.html
Summary: Who can join you in Italy, how the income test based on the assegno sociale works, what the housing check looks at, and why Blue Card holders can apply sooner.
For most of the people who write to us, the move is a family decision. A spouse with a career, children in school, sometimes an elderly parent. The question is rarely “can I work in Italy?” and more often “when can they come?”.
Italian law answers that in article 29 of the Immigration Act, and for Blue Card holders in article 27-quater, paragraph 16. Here is how it works in practice.
Who can join you   Article 29, paragraph 1 lists four groups:
your spouse, not legally separated and at least 18 years old; minor children, unmarried, including your spouse’s children and children born outside marriage, with the other parent’s consent where required; adult children who depend on you because of a health condition causing total disability; dependent parents who have no other children in the home country, or parents over 65 whose other children cannot support them for documented serious health reasons. Partners who are not married, siblings and other relatives are not on the list.
The income test   You must show lawful annual income of at least the yearly amount of the assegno sociale, the Italian social allowance, increased by half of that amount for each family member joining. If you are bringing two or more children under 14, the minimum is twice the yearly assegno sociale. Income of relatives living with you also counts.
We do not quote the 2026 amount of the assegno sociale here until we have read it on the INPS notice. The point is how to prove income: an Italian employment contract, monthly payslips and, later, the annual CU certificate are the standard evidence. When we are your employer, we provide all three.
The housing check   You also need a home that meets health and hygiene standards and is suitable for the number of people who will live in it. The municipality checks it. If a child under 14 is joining one parent, the owner’s consent is enough.
Two practical consequences. A small studio that is perfect for you alone may fail the check for a family of four. And a temporary furnished flat may be fine for your first weeks but not for the reunification file. Choose the long-term lease with the final family size in mind.
The Blue Card advantage   For ordinary permits, timing and conditions of reunification depend on the type and length of the permit. For a Blue Card, article 27-quater says reunification is available whatever the duration of the permit. Family members receive a permit of the same length as yours, which can later be converted into a work, self-employment or study permit if they meet the conditions.
In practice this means you can start the family file as soon as your own permit and housing are in place, without waiting for a minimum period of residence.
Documents: start now   The family file is document-heavy and slow: marriage certificate, birth certificates of the children, proof of dependency for parents. Documents issued outside the EU need legalisation or apostille and a certified Italian translation. Check that names and dates match exactly across all of them and the passports.
Start collecting them when the job offer is likely, not when you land.
Beyond the permit   School. Public schools teach in Italian; international schools exist in the larger cities. School and housing choices are linked. Health. Each family member enrols in the national health service once they hold a permit. Tax code. Every family member needs one. Your payslip. Fringe benefits are tax-free up to €2,000 a year for employees with dependent children in 2026, against €1,000 otherwise. Ask the company employing you whether it uses them. What your employer abroad can do   Pay a salary that leaves room for the income test, and agree a relocation budget that includes family travel and temporary housing. Everything else, from employment letters to payslips, we provide as the Italian employer.
See our family reunification page , or tell us about your family and we will map the steps.
What readers ask   Can my spouse come at the same time as me? It depends on the route and timing. Often the main applicant goes first, sets up housing and income evidence, then the family file starts. Ask us whether joint timing is possible in your case.
Does my spouse’s income count? Income of relatives living with you can count toward the test, according to article 29.
Do children need Italian to start school? No, but schools will expect them to learn it. Many schools offer support for new arrivals; ask the school directly.
What if my income changes later? Reunification is checked at the time of the application. Keep your payslips and CU certificates: they are also needed when family permits are renewed.

## Your First Weeks in Italy: Stay Contract, Residence Permit and the Questura
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/residence-permit-first-weeks-italy-blue-card.html
Summary: After landing on a work visa you have a short list of appointments to clear. What each one is, who goes, and what to bring.
The visa in your passport says you may enter Italy to work. It does not, on its own, let you stay. The first weeks after landing are about turning that entry into a residence permit, and getting the few registrations that make daily life work.
Here is the sequence, from our side as your employer and from yours.
1. The stay contract   Within days of arrival you and your employer go to the Sportello Unico per l’Immigrazione, the same immigration desk that issued the nulla osta. There you sign the contratto di soggiorno, the stay contract, which confirms the employment terms the permit was based on.
With an Employer of Record, we are the employer at that appointment. Bring your passport with the visa, and the documents the desk lists in the appointment letter. Confirm the exact deadline after entry for your case before you fly; deadlines are short.
2. The residence permit application   Next you apply for the permesso di soggiorno. For most work permits the application goes through the postal kit, available at designated post office counters. For a Blue Card the permit carries the wording “Carta blu UE” and lasts two years if your contract is permanent, or the length of the contract plus three months otherwise.
The post office gives you a receipt. Keep it with your passport: it shows the application is under way. Errors in the kit are the most common cause of delay: a name that does not match the passport exactly, a missing signature, an address where you cannot receive mail. Have someone who knows the forms check yours.
3. The Questura appointment   The police headquarters, the Questura, calls you to take fingerprints and a photo. Waiting times depend heavily on the city. Watch your phone and mail: a missed appointment can push the process back. The plastic card arrives later; until then the receipt is your evidence.
Whether the receipt allows you to start working while the card is produced depends on the route; we confirm it for your specific case before your first working day.
4. Tax code   The codice fiscale identifies you for tax, payroll, health care, leases and bank accounts. It is often issued before arrival or at the immigration desk. If not, the tax agency issues it. Payroll cannot run without it.
5. Residence registration   Once you have an address, register it at the municipal registry (anagrafe). Residence registration matters for health care, a driving licence, tax residence and many everyday services. Short-term accommodation may not be accepted for registration, which is one more reason to move into a proper lease soon. See housing for newcomers .
6. Health service   With the permit application and the tax code you can enrol in the national health service and choose a family doctor. This covers you for public health care; your employer does not need to buy private insurance, although some collective agreements add a supplementary fund.
7. Bank account   Your salary is paid by bank transfer to an Italian or EU account. Opening one usually needs the tax code, a passport, and proof of address or the permit receipt.
Who does what   Task You Employer (us) Stay contract Attend, sign Attend, sign, prepare employer documents Postal kit Fill in, submit Check, provide contract and employer data Questura Attend Track the case Tax code Request if missing Use it for payroll Hire notification - File electronically before you start Permit expiry - Track and start the renewal early The renewal, already now   Put the expiry date of the permit in your calendar on the day you receive it. The renewal should start well before expiry, and it is checked against the same contract and salary. Because we run your payroll, we see any change that could matter before it becomes a problem.
In short   Stay contract, postal kit, Questura, tax code, residence, doctor, bank. Seven steps, most in the first two weeks. Our relocation page has the checklist, and our team goes through it with you in Italian or English.
Points people get wrong   Can I travel abroad before the card arrives? Travel while the card is being produced has specific rules and risks. Check with us before booking any trip in the first weeks.
What if I move flat during the process? Update your address with the Questura and the post office, or you may miss the appointment letter.
Does my family follow the same steps? Yes, once they arrive with their own visa: their own permit application, tax codes, residence and health registration.

## How to Plan a Realistic Start Date for an Italian Work Visa
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/plan-italy-visa-timeline-start-date.html
Summary: The permit sets the start date, not the other way round. A backwards plan for Blue Card and quota cases, with the steps that usually slip.
The most common mistake in an international move is promising a start date before the permit route is clear. The candidate resigns, gives notice on the flat, books flights, and then the file waits for a document from a university registry on another continent.
Here is how to build the plan backwards, with honest buffers.
Start from the route   Everything depends on whether the case is a Blue Card or a quota permit .
Blue Card: no quota, and a legal 30-day deadline for the nulla osta. The variable parts are your documents and the consulate. Quota permit: you depend on application windows set by the Decreto Flussi and on places being available for your nationality group. The calendar of the decree drives everything. The pieces of a Blue Card timeline   Think of the timeline as five blocks.
Documents. Degree certificate, transcripts, experience letters, passport, and for the family marriage and birth certificates. Documents issued outside the EU usually need legalisation or apostille and a certified Italian translation. A CIMEA comparability statement can replace the declaration of value for degrees. This block is often the longest, and it is entirely in your hands: start it the day the offer is likely. Contract and filing. The Italian employer drafts the contract and files the request. With an Employer of Record this takes days, not weeks, once the salary and role are fixed. Nulla osta. Up to 30 days by law. Consulate. Appointment availability varies widely by country and city. Remember that the nulla osta has a limited life for the visa application (six months according to the Embassy in Beijing), so do not let it sit. Arrival. Stay contract, residence permit application, tax code, registration. The start date can be set once the stay contract is booked. We do not publish average durations for blocks 4 and 5 yet, because they vary by consulate and by city in Italy; we will add figures from our own cases when we have enough of them.
Buffers that are worth it   Two weeks between visa and flight. Visa collection, last bank and tax tasks at home, packing. A soft first week in Italy. The first days go to appointments. Starting payroll on day one is possible, but plan the workload lightly. A range, not a date. Tell the employer and your current landlord a window. Narrow it as each block closes. What slips most   A degree certificate whose name spelling differs from the passport. An experience letter that lists dates but not tasks and level, which weakens a Blue Card based on experience. A salary changed after filing, for example to add a bonus, which then does not match the application. Family documents started late, which delays the reunification file. Working while you wait   Waiting for the visa does not mean losing income. If your current employer is the one sending you to Italy, you keep working from your home country until the move. If it is a new employer, a short notice overlap with the old job can often be arranged. What you should not do is start working from Italy on a tourist entry: that creates immigration, tax and contribution problems for you and the company.
The quota case   For a quota permit, add a layer at the start: the application window and the allocation of places. Prepare everything before the window opens. If the place does not come through, the next allocation may be months away, so keep the Blue Card option under review: a salary adjustment can sometimes move a case from one route to the other.
Summary   Route first, documents second, filing third. Count the consulate and arrival as the variable parts. Give everyone a range. Tell us about your case and we will propose a timeline with the documents to start today.
The usual next questions   Should I resign before the visa? Only when the nulla osta is issued and the consular appointment is booked. Until then, keep your options open.
Can the employer pay me during the wait? If you already work for the company, yes, under your current contract at home. The Italian contract starts with the stay contract in Italy.
Who tracks the deadlines? We do, from the filing to the permit renewal. You get a single timeline with dates and owners for each step, updated as each block closes.
What if the consulate has no appointments? Tell us immediately. The nulla osta has a limited life, and we can check whether the consulate offers priority slots or alternative ways to submit.

## Blue Card or Quota Permit? Choosing the Right Italian Work Visa in 2026
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/blue-card-or-quota-permit-italy-2026.html
Summary: Italy has 43,300 non-seasonal quota places for 2026, but qualified professionals can skip the quota entirely. How to tell which route fits your profile.
Ask ten people how to get an Italian work visa and at least half will tell you about the “click day”, the morning when quota applications open and employers race to file. For many professionals that is the wrong mental model. The quota system is real, but a large share of the people we work with never touch it, because they qualify for the EU Blue Card.
This article explains both routes and how to choose.
The quota route in 2026   Ordinary work permits for non-EU nationals sit inside annual entry quotas set by the Decreto Flussi. The current framework is the DPCM of 2 October 2025, which plans entries for 2026, 2027 and 2028.
For 2026 the non-seasonal quota is 43,300 entries, split as follows, according to a secondary source we have not yet checked against the decree text:
25,000 for nationals of the countries listed in article 6, paragraph 2, letter a; 18,000 for nationals of countries with cooperation agreements with Italy; 300 for stateless persons and refugees. Three things follow. Your nationality decides which pool you draw from, so check it before anything else. The places are shared by every employer in Italy, so applications must be ready before the window opens. And a candidate whose country is in neither group may have no realistic quota route at all.
The Blue Card route   The Blue Card sits outside the quota. There is no click day, and the immigration desk has a legal 30-day deadline to issue the work authorisation or refuse it.
In exchange, it asks more of the candidate and the job:
Qualification: a degree of at least three years, a regulated profession with recognition, five years of qualified experience, or for ICT roles three years of experience in the last seven. Contract: at least six months. Salary: at least the CCNL level for the role and at least the ISTAT average gross annual salary, reported at about €36,300. A quick decision table   Your situation Likely route Graduate, salary above the threshold, contract of 6 months or more Blue Card ICT specialist without a degree, 3+ years of recent experience, salary above the threshold Blue Card Technician with 5+ years of qualified experience, salary above the threshold Blue Card, if the experience can be documented Salary below the threshold Quota permit Contract shorter than 6 months Quota permit, or a different structure Why salary is usually the deciding factor   Most of the professionals who write to us have the qualification. What decides the route is the gross salary the employer is willing to pay in Italy. Two warnings here.
First, the threshold is checked on gross annual salary (the Italian RAL), not on net pay and not on the employer’s total cost. Employer contributions, TFR and benefits do not count towards it.
Second, the salary must be the one actually paid. If the permit is granted at a certain salary and payroll later pays less, the permit is exposed. With an Employer of Record, the same team files the permit and runs payroll, so the two numbers cannot drift apart.
Both routes need an Italian employer   Neither route works without an employer in Italy. A foreign company can open an Italian entity, but that adds months before the permit even starts. An Employer of Record files the application, signs the stay contract and employs you from day one, while your company abroad sets the work.
What to do this week   Write down your qualification and years of relevant experience. Ask the employer for a gross annual salary in euros. Compare it with the Blue Card conditions . If it falls short, check your nationality against the quota groups . Send us the details : we reply with the route and the cost within one business day. What people ask us next   Can I switch from a quota permit to a Blue Card later? If your salary and qualification later meet the conditions, a new application on the Blue Card basis is possible. Ask us when your situation changes.
Does the quota apply to my family? Family reunification follows its own rules under article 29 and is not part of the work quota.
Is the click day still a thing? Quota applications open in set windows defined by the decree. We prepare the file in advance so it can be filed as soon as the window opens.
What if both routes fail? Sometimes the honest answer is that the role needs restructuring: a longer contract, a higher guaranteed salary, or a candidate who already holds the right to work in Italy. We would rather tell you early than file a weak case.
The lowest all-inclusive Employer of Record price for Italy ItalyBlueCard: €250 per employee per month, all included: Italian employment contract and CCNL selection, monthly payroll, payslips and filings, onboarding and offboarding, HR documents and amendments, invoicing in your currency at the EUR reference rate, no FX spread, no setup fee.

## EU Blue Card for Italy, Step by Step: From Job Offer to First Payslip
URL: https://italybluecard.com/articles/eu-blue-card-italy-step-by-step.html
Summary: The Italian Blue Card in the order things actually happen: eligibility, contract, nulla osta, consulate, stay contract and residence permit, with the sponsor problem solved by an EOR.
You have the offer, or at least a company that wants you. You have a degree or years of solid experience. You would like to live in Italy. Between that moment and your first Italian payslip there are five documents, three offices and one recurring question: who, exactly, is your employer in Italy?
This guide follows the EU Blue Card (Carta blu UE) in the order things happen. The legal basis is article 27-quater of the Italian Immigration Act (D.Lgs. 286/1998), rewritten in 2023 to implement the revised EU Blue Card directive, with operating instructions in a joint circular of the Ministry of Labour and the Ministry of the Interior of 28 March 2024.
Step 0: settle who the employer is   The Blue Card is requested by an employer in Italy. The application goes to the Sportello Unico per l’Immigrazione, the immigration desk at the local prefecture. A company in Bangalore, São Paulo or Austin with no Italian presence cannot easily file it.
There are two ways around that. The company opens its own Italian entity, which takes months before the permit can even start. Or an Employer of Record (EOR) in Italy becomes the legal employer: it signs the Italian contract, files the permit and runs payroll, while the company abroad keeps directing your work. That is what ItalyBlueCard does.
Step 1: check eligibility   Article 27-quater accepts one of four qualification profiles:
a higher education qualification of at least three years, or a three-year post-secondary qualification at level 6 of the national framework; the recognition required for a regulated profession, such as nursing; a higher professional qualification with at least five years of relevant experience at a level comparable to a degree; for ICT managers and specialists, at least three years of relevant experience in the last seven years. Then two conditions on the job. The contract or binding offer must last at least six months. And the salary must reach both the level of the applicable collective agreement (CCNL) and the average gross annual salary published by ISTAT. A secondary source puts that figure at about €36,300 a year; we treat it as provisional until we read the official notice. Check the details on our Blue Card page .
Step 2: build the contract   The nulla osta is granted on a specific contract: role, level, salary, hours, place of work. Everything in the application has to match what you will later sign and what you will be paid. Typical mistakes are a job title that does not match the qualification, a salary quoted net instead of gross, or a fixed-term contract shorter than six months.
With an EOR, the company abroad decides role and pay; the EOR translates them into an Italian contract under the right CCNL and checks the threshold before filing.
Step 3: the nulla osta   The employer files the request online. The law sets a deadline: the immigration desk must issue the nulla osta, or notify a refusal, within 30 days. That is one of the main practical differences from the quota route, where you also depend on application windows and available places.
The nulla osta is not a visa. It is the authorisation that lets you apply for one. It also has a limited life for that purpose: the Italian Embassy in Beijing, for example, states it is valid for no more than six months after issue. Book the consular appointment as soon as it arrives.
Step 4: the visa   You apply at the Italian embassy or consulate for your place of residence, not necessarily your country of citizenship. Expect to bring the application form, photo, passport, the nulla osta, the original qualification documents with legalisation and Italian translation, and proof of accommodation in Italy. A CIMEA comparability statement can replace the declaration of value for degrees. Each consulate publishes its own checklist; follow that one, not a generic list.
Step 5: arrival, stay contract, residence permit   Once in Italy you and your employer sign the stay contract at the immigration desk. Then you apply for the residence permit with the “Carta blu UE” wording. The permit lasts two years if your contract is permanent, otherwise the length of the contract plus three months. Our relocation page lists the other first-week tasks: tax code, residence registration, health service, bank account.
Step 6: payroll   From your first day you are an Italian employee: monthly payslip, INPS contributions, 13th month, TFR, at least four weeks of paid leave. The company abroad gets one monthly invoice. With ItalyBlueCard that is €250 per month plus the actual employment cost, in EUR or USD at the EUR reference rate.
What changes after a year   In the first 12 months you do the job the card was issued for. A change of employer needs the prior approval of the local labour office, which counts as given if it does not reply within 15 days. If you lose your job you can look for another while unemployed. You can also run a self-employed activity alongside the qualified job. After that first year, the labour market restrictions fall away.
The short version   Settle the employer first. Check qualification, contract length and salary. File, then move fast on the consulate. Keep every document consistent. Use the cost calculator to show the company abroad what employing you in Italy will cost.
In brief, your questions   Is the Blue Card tied to one city? No. The threshold and the rules are national. The immigration desk that handles the file is the one for the place of work.
Can the company abroad pay part of my salary from home? For the permit, what counts is the Italian contract and the salary paid through Italian payroll. Splitting pay across countries complicates tax and the threshold check; we advise against it.
The lowest all-inclusive Employer of Record price for Italy ItalyBlueCard: €250 per employee per month, all included: Italian employment contract and CCNL selection, monthly payroll, payslips and filings, onboarding and offboarding, HR documents and amendments, invoicing in your currency at the EUR reference rate, no FX spread, no setup fee.

## Cost of Sponsoring an Employee in Italy
URL: https://italybluecard.com/calculator.html
Summary: What it costs a company abroad to employ a visa holder in Italy: gross salary, employer contributions, INAIL, TFR and the EOR fee, month by month, in EUR and USD.
 Cost calculator What employing a visa holder in Italy costs Enter the gross salary you plan to offer. For a Blue Card it must also reach the salary threshold. The table shows the full employer cost under two example collective agreements; the visa fee of €2,500 per case is separate.
Annual gross salary, RAL (EUR) Collective agreement (CCNL)Commerce and services (CCNL Terziario, Distribuzione e Servizi)Engineering and manufacturing (CCNL Metalmeccanico Industria) Spread the 13th and 14th month pro rata over each month Pay TFR monthly into the employee’s chosen fund USD per EUR ItemPer month (avg)Per year Example figures, rates updated 2026-10-26. Contribution and insurance rates are indicative estimate and depend on the exact sector, company size and job risk class. We confirm them in your quote.
Your monthly invoices over a year The annual cost is the same either way. The options change when you pay it: with both options on, every month costs the same and nothing accumulates for later.
MonthSalaryINPS + INAILTFRFeeInvoice What the employment cost is made of RALAnnual gross salary. The figure in the offer letter. It is paid in 13 or 14 monthly installments depending on the CCNL: the extra installments are the 13th month (December) and, in commerce and services, the 14th month (July). INPSEmployer social security. Pension, unemployment, sickness and maternity funds, roughly 29–32% of gross pay. The employee pays a further ~9% out of their gross salary; that part is not an extra cost for you. INAILWorkplace injury insurance. Mandatory. Low for office jobs (well under 1%), higher for technical and production roles. TFRSeverance accrual. 6.91% of gross pay set aside every year and paid to the employee when employment ends, for any reason (Civil Code art. 2120). FeeOur EOR fee. €250 per employee per month. Billed on actuals, month by month The table above is an estimate. Each month we run the real payroll and invoice what it actually cost: overtime, bonuses, unpaid leave, sick days partly covered by INPS, salary changes and CCNL raises all show up in that month's figures. You receive the payslip summary with every invoice, so you can check every line.
Billing terms: one month's estimated cost as a deposit, plus the first month paid in advance; each month is then adjusted to the actual payroll on the next invoice.
Two collective agreements, compared On the same €50,000 RAL, an engineering contract under the Metalmeccanico agreement costs the employer roughly €1,500–2,000 a year more than an office contract under Commerce and services: social security rates are about 2–3 points higher and injury insurance is higher for technical roles. The Commerce agreement pays in 14 installments, so each monthly payslip is smaller, but the annual cost is the same RAL.
Which agreement applies is not a free choice: it follows the job and the sector of the work. We pick it in the contract draft and explain why.
Why the city changes net pay, not your cost On top of national income tax (IRPEF), every employee pays a regional surcharge (from 1.23% up to about 3.33% of taxable income, depending on the region and income band) and a municipal one (usually 0–0.8%; 0.9% in Rome, 1% in Naples, up to 1.2% in Turin; many cities exempt lower incomes). Both are withheld from the employee's gross pay.
They do not change what you pay. They change what the employee takes home: on a €50,000 RAL, the gap between the cheapest and the most expensive combination of region and city is in the order of €1,000–1,500 a year of net pay. Worth knowing when a relocating employee chooses where to live.

## EU Blue Card for Italy
URL: https://italybluecard.com/eu-blue-card-italy.html
Summary: EU Blue Card in Italy: who qualifies, the salary rule, the 30-day nulla osta deadline, permit length, changing jobs, family and EU mobility. With an Employer of Record (EOR) as sponsor.
 Visa routes The EU Blue Card in Italy The Blue Card (Carta blu UE) is Italy's permit for highly qualified employees. It is not subject to the annual quotas and has a legal deadline for the work authorisation. It still needs an Italian employer: if your company has none, we are that employer.
Who qualifies Under art. 27-quater, par. 1 of the Immigration Act (D.Lgs. 286/1998, as amended by D.Lgs. 152/2023), one of these is enough:
A degreeA higher education qualification of at least three years, or a post-secondary qualification of at least three years (level 6 of the national framework).
A regulated professionThe recognition required for regulated professions (D.Lgs. 206/2007), for example in health care.
Five years of experienceA higher professional qualification backed by at least five years of relevant experience at a level comparable to a degree.
ICT: three yearsICT managers and specialists (ISCO-08 groups 133 and 25) with at least three years of relevant experience in the last seven years.
Contract and salary 6 monthsThe employment contract or binding job offer must last at least six months (par. 5, a). 30 daysThe immigration desk must issue the nulla osta, or notify a refusal, within 30 days of the application (par. 6). 2 yearsFor a permanent contract the permit lasts two years; otherwise the length of the contract plus three months (par. 11). After you arrive First 12 months. You do the job the card was issued for. Changing employer needs prior approval of the local labour office, considered granted if it does not answer within 15 days (par. 13). Losing your job. You can look for and take up another job while unemployed (par. 13-bis). Side activity. Self-employment is allowed alongside the qualified job (par. 13-ter). Equal treatment with Italian nationals, apart from labour market access in the first 12 months (par. 15). Family. Reunification is available whatever the length of your permit; family members get a permit of the same length (par. 16). See family reunification. Coming from another EU country. A Blue Card from another Member State lets you work in Italy for up to 90 days in any 180; after 12 months there (6 if moving from a second Member State) you can move to Italy without a visa, with a work authorisation filed within one month of entry (par. 17). Source: art. 27-quater D.Lgs. 286/1998, consolidated text; joint circular Ministry of Labour - Ministry of the Interior no. 2829 of 28 March 2024 (lavoro.gov.it). Read 4 Nov 2026.
How we run it CheckDegree or experience, salary against the threshold and the CCNL, role code. ContractWe draft the Italian contract or binding offer, with your employer abroad setting the role and pay. Nulla ostaWe file it as employer. Its validity for the visa application is limited (six months, per the Embassy in Beijing checklist), so the consular appointment is planned in advance. Visa and arrivalConsulate, stay contract, residence permit, then payroll from your first day. Check my eligibilityCompare with Germany and the Netherlands

## Family Reunification in Italy
URL: https://italybluecard.com/family-reunification-italy.html
Summary: Bringing your spouse, children or parents to Italy: who is eligible, the income and housing conditions under art. 29, and the Blue Card rules.
 Visa routes Bringing your family to Italy For most people the move only works if the family comes too. Italian law sets who can join, and the income and housing you must show. Blue Card holders can apply whatever the length of their permit.
Who can join (art. 29, par. 1) SpouseNot legally separated and at least 18 years old.
Minor childrenUnmarried, including the spouse's children or children born outside marriage, with the other parent's consent where required.
Adult childrenDependent adult children who cannot provide for themselves because of a health condition causing total disability.
ParentsDependent parents with no other children in the home country, or over 65 when the other children cannot support them for documented serious health reasons.
Conditions (art. 29, par. 3) ConditionWhat the law requires HousingA home meeting health and hygiene standards and suitable for the number of occupants, checked by the municipality. For a child under 14 joining one parent, the owner's consent is enough. Source: art. 29 D.Lgs. 286/1998, consolidated text; for Blue Card holders art. 27-quater par. 16 (text). Read 4 Nov 2026.
How your Italian payslip helps The income test is met with documented, lawful income. An Italian employment contract and monthly payslips from us are exactly that evidence, and the rental contract you sign in Italy supports the housing check. Family members receive their own permit, which for Blue Card holders lasts as long as yours and can later be converted into a work or study permit.
Start collecting marriage and birth certificates early: documents issued abroad need legalisation or apostille and a certified Italian translation. Choose the home with the family size in mind: the housing check counts occupants. Plan school places and health service registration for each family member. Plan the family moveRelocation steps

## FAQ on Visas and Employment in Italy
URL: https://italybluecard.com/faq.html
Summary: Answers on the EU Blue Card, work permits, family, relocation and Employer of Record (EOR) employment in Italy, for non-EU professionals and their employers.
 FAQ Questions we get every week Short answers for professionals and for the companies that employ them. Every case is different: ask us about yours.
Permits Why do I need an Italian employer?The work authorisation (nulla osta) is requested by an employer in Italy. A company abroad with no Italian entity cannot easily file it. As Employer of Record we are that employer.
Blue Card or quota permit?Blue Card if you have a three-year degree (or qualifying experience), a contract of at least six months and a salary at or above the threshold. Otherwise the quota route. See visa routes.
What is the Blue Card salary threshold?How fast is the nulla osta?For the Blue Card the law sets 30 days from the application. Consular and arrival steps come on top.
Are there quotas for the Blue Card?No. The 2026 quotas (43,300 non-seasonal entries) apply to ordinary work permits.
Can I change employer?With a Blue Card, in the first 12 months only with prior approval of the labour office (deemed granted after 15 days). Then freely.
I have a Blue Card in another EU country. Can I move?You can work in Italy up to 90 days in 180. After 12 months in the first country you can move to Italy without a visa, with a work authorisation filed within a month of entry.
Family and relocation When can my family join?Blue Card holders can apply whatever the length of their permit. Income and housing conditions apply: see family reunification.
Can my spouse work?Do you help with housing?Yes, as part of the relocation service, quoted per case.
Costs What does the employer pay?€250 per month plus the actual employment cost, and €2,500 per visa case.
Which currencies?EUR, or USD at the EUR reference rate with no FX spread.
How much more than salary?Employer contributions around 30%, plus 13th month and TFR. Use the calculator.
Is there a deposit?One month's estimated cost, plus the first month in advance.
Employment Is it a real Italian contract?Yes, under the CCNL of the sector, with the same rights as any employee in Italy.
Do I need private health insurance?Residents with a work permit enrol in the national health service. Some CCNLs add a supplementary fund.
Who owns my work?The company you work for: our contracts include an IP assignment and confidentiality clause in its favour.
What if the company later opens an Italian entity?We transfer you without loss of seniority. Your permit is updated with the new employer.
Ask a questionEstimate a cost

## For Professionals Moving to Italy
URL: https://italybluecard.com/for-talent.html
Summary: For non-EU professionals employed in Italy through ItalyBlueCard: your permit, your Italian contract, payslip, INPS pension, TFR, 13th month, leave and family.
 For professionals You are moving to Italy, with us as your employer A company abroad wants you on its team, in Italy. We are your legal employer here: we sponsor your permit, sign your Italian contract and pay you every month. Your work, your manager and your goals stay with the company that chose you.
Your permitWe file the nulla osta, sign the stay contract with you and track the renewal of your residence permit, so it never expires unnoticed.
Your contractA written Italian contract under the CCNL for your sector, with level, salary, hours and probation, in Italian and English.
Your payslipMonthly, with tax and contributions already withheld. It is also the income evidence you need for a lease and for bringing your family.
Pension and healthYour contributions go to INPS and build your Italian pension. You enrol in the national health service like any resident.
TFR and 13th monthAbout 6.91% of your yearly pay set aside as TFR severance, and an extra month's pay in December (a 14th in summer under some CCNLs).
LeaveAt least 4 weeks of paid holiday, public holidays, paid sick leave, maternity and paternity leave.
Questions from people on the move Who is my employer on paper?ItalyBlueCard is your legal employer in Italy and the sponsor of your permit. The company abroad directs your daily work.
What if I want to change job?With a Blue Card, in the first 12 months a change of employer needs prior approval of the labour office, deemed granted after 15 days without reply. After that you move like any employee.
What if the company abroad ends the project?Italian dismissal rules and notice apply. As a Blue Card holder you can look for another job while unemployed, and you receive TFR, unused leave and the accrued 13th month.
Can my family come?Yes, under the income and housing conditions. See family reunification.
Do I file a tax return?Tax is withheld through payroll and you receive the CU certificate every year. You file a return only for other income or deductions.
Who helps me when I land?One contact in our team, in Italian or English, from the visa appointment to your first payslip. See relocation.
Your future employer has not heard of us yet? Send them this page.

You have an Italian entity You have no Italian entityThere is no Italian group company to receive the transfer. We hire the person in Italy as Employer of Record, usually under the Blue Card, and your company keeps directing the work.

## Italian Employment Contracts for Visa Holders
URL: https://italybluecard.com/italy-employment-contracts.html
Summary: The Italian employment contract behind a work permit: CCNL, contract terms, leave, sickness, parental leave, public holidays and termination.
 Employment guide The contract behind the permit The permit is granted on the basis of a specific contract: role, level, salary and hours. Whatever is written there must match what happens on the payslip, from the first month to the renewal.
Contract and CCNL Every contract is written and sits under a national collective agreement (CCNL) chosen by job and sector. The CCNL sets the minimum pay for each level, hours, overtime, leave, probation and notice. For a Blue Card the salary must also reach the ISTAT-based threshold, and the contract must last at least six months.
The contract states title and level, place of work, salary, hours, start date, probation and whether it is permanent or fixed-term. A permanent contract gives a two-year Blue Card; a fixed-term one gives a card for the contract length plus three months.
Changes such as a raise or a promotion go into a written amendment. A pay cut below the threshold or a change of role can affect the permit: talk to us before any change.
Ending employment A valid reason, the CCNL notice period, and TFR and unused leave in the final payslip. Probation, up to 6 months depending on the CCNL, is when either side can end it freely.
Leave and absences Annual leave: at least 4 weeks a year, often more under the CCNL, plus paid hours off (ROL) in many agreements. Useful for the long trips home many relocated employees plan. Sick leave: the doctor sends the certificate online to INPS; pay is shared between INPS and employer under the CCNL. Maternity and paternity: 5 months of mandatory maternity leave and 10 working days of paternity leave, mostly paid through INPS. Public holidays: 12 national holidays plus the local patron saint's day. More in the guide EOR, entity or contractors? The payroll calendar From RAL to net pay Contracts, leave and termination Running payroll from abroad Get a quote
